articles.full_text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ben Bernstein, and Andrew Brandt for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Huntress is tracking N-able's response to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in its N-central platform, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform built for managed service providers and IT teams. On November 9, N-able took its hosted N-central environment offline while it worked to secure the environment and apply remediation.

That move came after an independent researcher published the details of 33 critical vulnerabilities to GitHub that can be chained to lead to four different exploits (dubbed "Able2Shell"). Three of those chained exploits lead to remote code execution and one leads to privilege escalation to root. The vulnerabilities impact servers running N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 (and likely earlier versions as well).

N-able said it has not seen active exploitation of the vulnerabilities as of November 9 at 15:15:00 UTC. The company is working on a hotfix that it said will be available soon; customers should keep their N-central servers offline until N-able confirms they can be brought back online safely.

Huntress has tracked and responded to other, separate flaws in N-able's N-central this year, including five critical CVEs:

August 2026: N-able released a hotfix for CVE-2026-18556, a critical vulnerability impacting all current versions of N-central across both hosted and on‑prem deployments, giving attackers unauthenticated, "god-mode" access to the RMM console. CVE-2026-18577 was disclosed soon after as an incomplete patch to the former CVE.

September 2026: N-able issued a hotfix to address a third vulnerability, CVE-2026-86218, an actively exploited pre-auth RCE zero day with a 10.0 CVSS score. The next day Huntress produced a proof of concept (PoC) exploit of a separate, net new vulnerability chain (CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207) in N-central that allowed attackers to bypass access controls to create unauthorized administrative accounts.

What Should Potentially Impacted Organizations Do?

Potentially impacted organizations should do the following:

If you run N-central on premises, take the server offline now and keep it offline until N-able confirms it is safe to restore.

If you use N-able's hosted service, expect an outage. N-able has taken its cloud infrastructure offline; follow its status page for updates.

Review login and authentication activity from November 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access. If you find suspicious activity, involve your incident-response team and assess whether systems or client networks managed through N-central may also be affected. The document warns that exploitation could enable remote code execution or privilege escalation on the server.

Carefully examine your audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise. During previous N-central vulnerability exploitations (such as the CVE-2026-86218 zero-day), threat actors were observed "spraying" downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools. Specifically, you should monitor for anomalous remote access sessions, new scripts being deployed, or the unauthorized creation of new administrator accounts.

Apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe. The document said a hotfix was in development, with no exact ETA, so check current vendor guidance rather than relying on this dated update.

N-able does not always iterate version numbers when it pushes down live hotfixes that don't require a reboot, so it remains to be seen whether the patched version will be numbered 2026.4.0.31 or something different.

Next Steps

Huntress is actively investigating this incident and we are communicating with our potentially vulnerable customers to share updates as they become available. Please check this blog for further updates as we learn more information.

You can also get further updates from N-able at: https://uptime.n-able.com/event/202561/

articles.title: Inside an AhsayCBS Intrusion: Hidden Webshells, a CryptoMiner, and a C2 Implant

articles.full_text:
Background

In early October, Huntress began seeing threat actors exploit two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console for Ahsay's backup software: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-105134, unauthenticated remote code execution as SYSTEM through /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Our original blog post covered the first wave: webshells, an XMRig miner dressed up as Microsoft Edge, and a script that hid the miner from Task Manager. Ahsay has since released hotfixes (10.3.4.45 for v10, and 9.15.2.70 for v7 through v9), and we verified that 10.3.4.45 blocks the entry point we saw.

The impacted organization's servers in this post were exploited between October 8 and October 11, 2026, which was before Ahsay released its hotfixes. During our investigation into the attack, we analyzed webshells, loaders, and an implant that the threat actor used during the attack.

This activity matches the campaign in our first post. We tied it to AhsayCBS exploitation because the webshells sat inside AhsayCBS's own web directories, the AhsayCBS access logs show an exploit source address that is listed in that post, and one of the servers also held files matching that post's indicators.

When organizations apply hotfixes, it mitigates the issue moving forward, but if a compromise has already happened it does not remove files an actor has already planted. If your AhsayCBS servers were exposed before patching, it's worth searching your environment for the artifacts in this post.

What we found, at a glance

Our initial report described incidents that involved a quick smash and grab: a webshell or a few commands, then a miner. However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups. The rest of this post takes apart the pieces one at a time.

Figure 1: An overview of what the operator left on the exploited servers

Webshells, in several flavors

Overall, we saw five webshell families during our investigation (seen in the table below), all with varying parameters and characteristics.

One of the most common webshells we found in this environment was small in size: it compared a hardcoded key in the p parameter against its own copy and returned a plain 404 if the key is wrong, so a scanner that does not know the key would see an empty page. With the right key, the c parameter would be passed to cmd.exe /c and the output would come back Base64-encoded.

The second webshell family included w and d parameters, which were designed to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and make it easy to drop more tools. Every file carried its own key (always 12 hex characters followed by a capital P).

The third family looked completely different, and included files named status_ followed by six random letters. These shells used auth, cmd, del, and rm parameters: they were designed to run commands, recursively delete any path they are given, and delete themselves. To the latter point, defenders should keep in mind that the shell can delete itself after use, so not finding the file on disk does not prove it was never present.

A smaller variant of this family, named st_ followed by six random letters, drops the authentication and the delete function. It takes c with no authentication at all, plus a get=env parameter that prints the application home, the Catalina base, the operating system and the temp directory, and an rm=1 parameter that deletes the file.

Family

p key (a wrong key returns 404), c command run through cmd.exe /c, output Base64-encoded. a and b return a sum, which works as a quick liveness check.

The folder locations where we found these webshells gave us further insight into how the attack might vary across operating systems. The impacted servers here ran Windows: however, the exploit also attempted Linux-style installation paths, suggesting the exploit was not tailored to one operating system.

In addition to webapps\cbs and webapps\rps in the real install, we found copies in directories matching Linux-style paths, including /opt/AhsayCBS, /usr/local/AhsayCBS, and /home/ahsay/AhsayCBS. On one of the affected Windows servers, these appeared as folders under C:\opt, C:\usr, and C:\home, with a staging folder, C:\ahsay_tf, holding another copy. That suggests the exploit was not designed for a specific operating system or install path, and simply tried every likely location.

The copies outside the live install were not served by the web application, so they probably cannot be used as shells on Windows, but they are a reliable tell. Several shells also sat in random six-character folders, each containing its own app, conf, and webapps\cbs subfolders. These imitate the structure of an AhsayCBS install, but none of the components are part of the real application. Some of those folders held empty pb_ marker files in the conf folder, and folders named ahsay_poc_*, ahsay_tf, ahsay_th and ahsay_t0 showed up in Program Files.

Figure 2: Shell locations on a Windows host: the live install, and the Linux-style paths the exploit also tries

A webshell that hides inside an image

One of the webshell families, AhsayCBS.jsp (in webapps\rps), was disguised as an image-preview service: it was designed to extract encrypted code from uploaded PNGs and run it in memory while making its traffic resemble ordinary image requests.

The webshell's disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint. The webshell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later.

On the sample we saw, the webshell was designed to work as follows:

First, the operator POSTs a PNG.

Then the page reads the least-significant bit of each pixel's red, green and blue values, one pixel at a time.

It strings those bits together and packs them into bytes, with the first bit read becoming the most significant bit of each byte.

That rebuilds a four-byte big-endian length followed by that many bytes of payload, which it then decrypts with AES.

The key is hardcoded, and the cipher is Java's default AES transformation (translating to ECB mode with PKCS5 padding).

On the first request, the decrypted bytes are loaded as a Java class through a small custom ClassLoader and stored in the application context under the attribute name QuCh, and the page answers with its built-in cover image. On later requests, it creates an instance of that class, hands it the request, an output buffer and the decrypted data through calls to equals(), and calls toString() to run it. Whatever the class produces is encrypted again and written into a new PNG.

Passing arguments through equals() is a convention used by some open-source in-memory webshell frameworks, though we have not tied this one to a specific framework. The practical effect is that the functionality arrives per request and lives in memory. The access log showed what looked like image traffic, and there was no c or p parameter to search for. We analyzed the loader, not the class it receives, so we cannot confirm what the operator actually ran through it.

Figure 3: How AhsayCBS.jsp turns an uploaded image into running code

A webshell with a signed API

Not every shell was a one-liner. nsmind.jsp, also in webapps\rps, behaved like a small remote administration service.

In the sample we saw, every request must carry an X-Auth-Token header that matches a hardcoded API key, plus X-Timestamp, X-Nonce and an X-Signature header holding an HMAC-SHA256 of the request parameters. The timestamp has to be within five minutes of the server's clock, and each nonce is stored in the application context so a captured request cannot be replayed. A request that fails any check gets a short JSON error, so the page behaves like an ordinary API that rejects unauthenticated callers.

Behind the checks, the action parameter selects exec, cd, upload or download. exec runs the command through cmd.exe /c (after chcp 65001, so output comes back as UTF-8) and tracks the working directory between calls, so the operator gets a persistent shell. upload and download move files in chunks using an offset parameter, with a limit of 4 GB per file, which means a large file can be pulled off the server through many small requests.

On a server that holds backups, this download action is the part to worry about: it is a ready-made exfiltration channel that looks like normal API traffic. We did not see logs showing download in use, so we cannot say what, if anything, was taken.

The files also showed the operator iterating. In the same rps folder we found three timestamp-named folders, each holding a single copy of a shell. The oldest held the simple cmd, del and rm shell described above, and the two newer ones contained nsmind.jsp, which suggested the operator upgraded from a basic shell to this tool. We also found byte-identical copies of nsmind.jsp and AhsayCBS.jsp on two of the servers, which pointed to one operator or one script working across hosts.

A second miner, with its own persistence

The Edge-themed miner analyzed in our initial blog was not the only one: we also found another miner in our follow-up investigation.

The XMRig miner we observed (kvm-agent.exe) is configured like a standard XMRig build: donate level 0, MSR access enabled (the same capability the WinRing0 driver in the first post provides), and TLS connections on port 443 to SupportXMR pools. The wallet and password differed from the Kryptex pool and user listed in the first post, making us believe this was a separate miner and not a second copy of the first. We found the same file, with the same hash, on two servers, and the task on both was created the same night and edited within seconds of each other, which again points to one operator or one script working across hosts.

During our analysis, we found a scheduled task named kvm running as SYSTEM every minute. Its command used a tasklist to check whether kvm-agent.exe was running and, if it wasn't, it would start it from C:\Windows\SysWOW64\kvm-agent. This means that if the miner was killed, it would be back up and running within a minute. The task's start time was set well before the intrusion (making it look older than it was in task listings).

Figure 4: The kvm scheduled task (start time elided)

A Python implant that only runs where it was staged

The most interesting file we pulled was main.py, which sits in an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile and is started from a Run key through explorer.exe. The script is only a wrapper: Base64, then lzma, then a marshaled Python code object that it passes to exec. Decoding it without running it shows that the code was compiled from a file called heap_shellcode_runner_bound_weaponized.py.

The code computes the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a file with that name next to main.py. Based on the bytecode, if the marker file is missing, the script exits. That would keep the implant from running in a sandbox or on an analyst's machine, because the marker only exists on the host it was provisioned for. We did not find a marker file in the folder we collected, so either it was not part of what we pulled or it was removed. If the marker is present, the script copies a 673 KB blob into an executable heap (HeapCreate, HeapAlloc, RtlMoveMemory) and starts it on a new thread with CreateThread.

Figure 5: The implant's execution flow, reconstructed from static analysis

Figure 6: The decoded logic, reconstructed from the code object

The blob starts with a short bootstrap that calls a reflective loader at the end of the blob, which in turn maps an x64 DLL carried inside it. The DLL is C++ with a JSON library and imports very little: bcrypt, KERNEL32, OLEAUT32 and SHLWAPI, with the networking functions resolved at run time. It has no export table, no PDB path and no version resource, so the usual attribution breadcrumbs have been stripped.

Its strings include the C2 URL hxxps://creepexplosiondarknight[.]com/d, a JSON content type, a mutex, and string fragments (dns.quad with 9.net, and dns.goog) consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups through Quad9 and Google. It also reads MachineGuid and Windows version information, which fits host identification. We have not identified the malware family and have not watched the implant run, so what it does after it checks in is still an open question.

Figure 7: Selected strings from the embedded DLL (C2 defanged)

The rest of the toolkit

Around those pieces, the same environment held the tunneling tools gost and chisel, staged in .st<id> folders as wust<id>a.exe and wust<id>b.exe, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a local account named wdguest, and a Mimikatz package on disk. We also saw Microsoft Defender exclusions that covered C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows, temp folders, the dropper processes, and the AhsayCBS service process (cbssvcX64.exe). These exclusions would have reduced Defender's ability to scan files in those locations and files accessed by the excluded processes, creating broad blind spots for the operator's tooling.

Backup servers as a target

Everything above ran on servers whose purpose is to hold or manage backups. On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI. Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident.

What to check for

Patching closes the entry point. It does not clean up what already happened, so on any server that was exposed before the hotfix, look for:

Unexpected .jsp files under webapps\cbs and webapps\rps, especially random names and the status_ and st_ patterns, and requests to UpdateReceivers.do in the AhsayCBS access logs

Folders named ahsay_*, home, opt, srv or usr at the root of the drive or in Program Files, and timestamp-named folders (year-month-day-hour-minute-second) next to the shells, which in some cases held a single copy of one

Scheduled tasks and services you did not create, including a SYSTEM task with a one-minute repeat that tests for a process with tasklist

Defender exclusions you did not add, especially for C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows and the AhsayCBS service process

An embedded Python install under the SYSTEM profile and a Run key that launches it

A few behaviors make useful detections even when the files are gone:

python.exe or pythonw.exe running from a path under the SYSTEM profile

Outbound requests to public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers from a process that is not a browser

New .jsp files created under the AhsayCBS web directories

The parent-child pattern our earlier Sigma rule already looks for, where cbssvcX64.exe spawns a command shell.

If you find any of the above, we recommend a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network.

articles.title: Sasha Roshan Takes Security Education Beyond the Demo
articles.context: On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats
articles.full_text:
Sasha Roshan is a Senior Sales Engineer at Huntress and a cybersecurity educator. His work sits at the point where technical expertise meets real-world security needs. He helps customers and partners understand what they're trying to protect, and he asks the questions that reveal the real problem before showing how Huntress can help.

That can mean preparing a customer demonstration, helping a partner work through a technical scenario, presenting a webinar, supporting an event, or collaborating with colleagues on content and on building hacking environments. No two weeks look exactly the same, but the common thread is communication. The technical detail needs to be accurate, and it also needs to be relevant to the person in front of him.

"The best conversations are not product tours," Sasha says. "They're about helping someone understand what's happening in their environment and how the attack happens, what matters most, and what they can do next."

Sasha on BBC

What one partner actually needed to know

One partner conversation shows how Sasha approaches the work. A partner had questions about day-to-day operations, asking what would happen overnight and how their team could avoid drowning in false positives. Just as important was understanding who would make decisions when something serious was detected.

Sasha built the conversation around that operational journey and kept product terminology to a minimum. He walked through how the Huntress SOC handles detection and response, and how the service works alongside Microsoft Defender. He then showed what escalation looks like in practice. Once the discussion tracked the partner's real concerns, it moved from general interest to a concrete next step. Sasha and the team proposed a trial in the partner's environment and scheduled a follow-up to plan the deployment.

Sasha doing what he does best: Educating the community

Taking sales engineering beyond the one-to-one conversation

Sasha enjoys helping make that picture clearer, whether he's speaking with a customer or partner, presenting to a live audience, or recording a video for someone who's learning on their own.

His focus includes areas such as identity security and security posture management, where small gaps can create meaningful risk. On YouTube, he breaks down subjects that can sound intimidating, including security teams, attack techniques, and identity-based threats. Across every format, Sasha tries to take something complicated and leave people better equipped to protect themselves.

Doing that well means knowing the audience and being able to explain the same idea from more than one angle. Creating content sharpens Sasha's thinking, while speaking with live audiences helps him understand which explanations resonate. Both make him a better Sales Engineer.

Sharing knowledge, as usual

articles.title: Brute Force Sentry for Managed SIEM | Huntress
articles.context: Brute Force Sentry normalizes both into one authentication surface, so a single detection can follow the attack from the first failure to the login
articles.full_text:
Today, Huntress Managed SIEM's Brute Force Sentry is available to all Managed SIEM customers. It turns the brute force attacks our SOC sees in the field into detections that fire earlier, with the evidence and hardening guidance you need to close the gap. Brute Force Sentry watches your internet-facing login surfaces, including RDP, RD Gateway, and the RDWeb portal on Windows and SSH on Linux. When a run of failed logons ends in a successful one, the Huntress SOC investigates.

Every exposed login gets knocked on, and most of that knocking is bots cycling through "administrator" on a gateway someone set up years ago. The trouble is that one burst out of thousands ends in a working login, and a generic threshold rule treats it the same as the rest.

Brute Force Sentry is built to find that one.

RDP is still a front door attackers use

Huntress research ties RDP to 10–20% of how advanced attackers break into networks. Plenty of organizations don't realize their RDWeb portal or RD Gateway is reachable from the internet until someone starts working through usernames on it.

RDWeb and RD Gateway behave a lot like an SSL VPN portal. Authentication happens at the web portal, before the user ever reaches an endpoint, so that portal is where attackers line up.

Most SIEMs handle brute force with a single threshold rule, something like "X failed logons in Y minutes." Set it low and your team drowns in alerts from bots that never get in. Set it high and a slow spray across dozens of accounts slips right under it. In both cases, the rule can't answer the question you care about: did one of those attempts work?

How Brute Force Sentry works

Brute Force Sentry reads the authentication telemetry your Managed SIEM already collects across all three platforms: Windows Security events (4624, 4625, 4740, 4776) and RD Gateway's own connection log, Linux sshd, and macOS, and splits "brute force" into the distinct tradecraft it really is:

Traditional brute force: one source guessing against a few accounts until something works

Distributed brute force: many sources working the same account, each staying quiet enough on its own to look unremarkable

Spraying: a short list of common credentials tried across many accounts

Credential stuffing: username and password pairs from earlier breaches, tested to see which still work

Username enumeration: repeated attempts against accounts that don't exist, probing for valid names before the guessing starts

It reads each platform in its own language. Windows spreads a single authentication across several event IDs, with the failure reason buried in a status code and the credential check sometimes landing on a domain controller instead of the machine being attacked. Linux writes one sshd line that already separates a wrong password from an attempt against an account that was never real. Rather than flatten both into a lowest common denominator, we normalize them into one authentication record that keeps what each platform knows, so the detection logic is identical everywhere and nothing is lost in translation.

It's tuned per surface, not set once.. Each one gets its own narrow correlation detection in place of a single noisy rule. Our researchers tuned every detection per login surface against historical partner data, then validated it against simulated real-world attacks in the lab before the SOC got it.

It correlates across providers. The failed sign-ins and the success that follows are often recorded by two different systems on the same host. Brute Force Sentry normalizes both into one authentication surface, so a single detection can follow the attack from the first failure to the login.

It turns itself on, and tells you when it can't. Brute Force Sentry activates per organization once the telemetry it needs is flowing. If that telemetry is missing, it shows as unavailable along with the reason, so a quiet dashboard means Huntress checked and found nothing.

The accounts they go after aren't the ones you're watching

Across the compromises Huntress has worked, the accounts that fell weren't always domain admins. They were the ones nobody owns; shared logins created for a device, a front desk, or a one off integration, with a password nobody has rotated since and an MFA exemption nobody remembers granting. They don't surface on a privileged-account review, and they don't belong to anyone who'd notice them being used. That's exactly why attackers reach for them first, and the pattern holds whichever door they come through: a Windows desktop or gateway, a Linux server, or a Mac sharing its screen.

Brute Force Sentry surfaces the usernames being attempted, not just how many times. That includes the ones that don't exist. A run of failures against accounts that were never real is username enumeration, someone working a list, learning your naming convention before they start guessing passwords in earnest. Catching that tells you an attack is being set up rather than already underway. And seeing which real accounts an attacker keeps returning to tell you which credentials to rotate tonight, not next quarter.

About 1,700 attempts in 72 seconds

In June 2026, the Huntress SOC handled a compromise at an organization running Remote Desktop Gateway. The attacker hit eight accounts with 212 to 215 failed logons each, roughly 1,700 attempts in 72 seconds, and then got in.

Every one of those failures was sitting in the gateway host's event logs. The successful login that came right after was recorded by RD Gateway, a different provider on the same host. Connecting the two took a detection that didn't exist yet, and Brute Force Sentry was built to make that connection.

To see how often this pattern shows up, we reviewed 30 confirmed RDWeb/RDG compromises during the first four weeks of testing. In 20 of them, Brute Force Sentry's signal would have reached the SOC up to an hour earlier. That's an hour between the attacker's first guess and their first move inside the network, and it's an hour our analysts can spend containing the account.

An attacker who gets in through your gateway keeps moving, so the sooner you see the login, the less of the network they've touched.

What you'll see in the portal

Most brute force activity never succeeds, and until now partners haven't seen any of it. Brute Force Sentry shows it as it happens, so you can act on your own terms before something breaks through:

Exposed surfaces: which internet-facing login surfaces are under attack, including ones you may not have known were reachable

Targeted accounts: the accounts attackers keep coming back to

Sources: where the attempts come from, and which sources keep returning

Compromises: successful logins that followed a run of failures, each linked to its Incident Report

You're notified on compromise, and you can opt in to notifications for every attempt, successful or not.

Figure 1: Brute Force Sentry dashboard

Less noise for you, more proof for your customers

If you're an MSP, you've probably told a client their RD Gateway needs MFA or belongs behind a VPN. Brute Force Sentry gives you their own data to make that case, starting with whether the portal should be exposed at all: which accounts were targeted last week, how many attempts were made, and where they came from. Pair that with the hardening guidance in each finding, and the conversation moves from "we should" to "here's what happened."

Internal IT teams get the same benefit. You don't have to become a Windows event log specialist to tell whether a burst of 4625s was background noise or the start of an intrusion, because the Huntress SOC is already looking at the ones that matter.

Built from the attacks our SOC works

Brute Force Sentry started with a real incident and a gap our analysts could name. That's how we want Managed SIEM to keep growing: take the attacks our SOC sees in partner environments and turn them into detections that fire earlier, with the evidence attached.

Every exposed login gets knocked on. Now you'll know which knock got answered.

Already on Huntress Managed SIEM? It's included for all Managed SIEM customers and turns on automatically once your Windows authentication telemetry is flowing. New to Managed SIEM? Book a demo to see Brute Force Sentry and the Huntress SOC in action.

articles.title: Adversary Infrastructure New Huntress ITDR Feature
articles.context: It stopped 305 attack attempts at the door
articles.full_text:
It started with a fire drill

In March, our SOC watched a phishing-as-a-service operation turn Railway, a developer cloud platform with a spotless IP reputation, into a token-harvesting engine. Device code phishing lures hit 344 organizations across five countries in under three weeks. Microsoft had no reason to score those logins as risky. That was the whole point.

So we did something we'd never done before. We hand-built a Conditional Access policy blocking Railway's IP ranges, validated it against 14 days of fleet traffic, and pushed it to every eligible Managed ITDR tenant. It stopped 305 attack attempts at the door. Zero legitimate logins were affected.

Then the attackers moved to new infrastructure. They always do.

That's the problem we built Adversary Infrastructure to solve. It's the newest capability in Huntress Managed ITDR, and it turns that one-time emergency response into continuous protection. When one tenant gets hit, every tenant gets the block. We call it herd immunity for identity.

Attackers are renting clean infrastructure and scaling with AI

The Railway campaign told us something about how identity attacks work now. Across 344 victims, we found no two identical phishing lures. Each one was tailored enough to slip past email filtering. That kind of variety at that kind of volume means automation or AI is writing the lures. The group behind it, EvilTokens, sells a storefront with AI workflows for bypassing filters, personalizing pretexts, and hunting inboxes for wire fraud targets. It even has a 24/7 support desk.

The infrastructure side has changed too. Attackers don't need to buy bulletproof hosting anymore. They rent clean, cheap, trusted cloud space, stand up a token relay in minutes, and tear it down when it's burned. Developer platforms, VDI tunnels, and AiTM relays all look legitimate to Microsoft's risk scoring until someone proves otherwise.

The scale is hard to overstate. In a single 14-day window, 5,086 distinct attacker IP addresses hit the Huntress fleet. Partners can't curate blocklists at that pace. Nobody can, by hand.

What Adversary Infrastructure is

Adversary Infrastructure blocks attackers at the Microsoft 365 sign-in, before they ever get a session.

Figure 1: Adversary Infrastructure in the Huntress Platform

When the Huntress SOC confirms the hosting, relay, or proxy infrastructure behind a compromise in one tenant, we turn it into a blocking Conditional Access policy in every eligible, opted-in tenant. Attacks from that infrastructure fail at sign-in instead of becoming incidents you have to clean up.

It's precision blocking, sourced from real attacks we've already investigated across the 17M+ identities we protect. Only the IP ranges that are bad, nothing else. Huntress maintains it end to end. There's no blocklist for you to curate, no policy for you to write, no threat feed for you to consume. And it's included in Managed ITDR for Microsoft 365 at no extra cost.

How it works

The whole loop runs from one confirmed incident to fleet-wide blocking, often the same day.

The SOC confirms a compromise with a real incident in a real tenant, with the hosting, relay, or proxy addresses behind it.

Detection engineers validate the infrastructure. It has to be datacenter or hosting space, scoped tightly to the evidence, with zero legitimate logins anywhere across the fleet and confirmed reports from at least two unrelated partners. A second engineer reviews every nomination. If real users log in from an address, it doesn't ship.

Huntress deploys the block. New campaigns go to our own canary tenants first. Then one blocking policy with one named location per campaign - each labeled [HUNTRESS] - roll out to every eligible, opted-in tenant.

Figure 2: Conditional Access policies by campaign in Adversary Infrastructure

The next attack fails at sign-in. No token is issued. The attack never becomes an incident.

You get the receipt. Every block produces a Low severity incident report naming the targeted identity, source, and campaign, and the credential the attacker tried to use gets rotated.

We check every tenant daily, repair drift, and update ranges as attackers rotate. We never touch policies you authored. Tenants that can't run Conditional Access still get the same detections and incident reports, just after the sign-in instead of before.

Two campaigns that brought you Adversary Infrastructure

Every campaign we've turned into fleet-wide protection started as somebody's very bad day. Here are two.

LSHIY LLC: 81 million login attempts from one IPv6 range. Three months after Railway, our SOC spotted a password spray replaying validated credentials through ROPC, a legacy auth flow that skips the MFA prompt entirely. It compromised 78 accounts across 64 organizations. Here's the part that stung: 55 of those accounts had active Conditional Access policies requiring MFA. The policies looked right. They just didn't cover the flow the attacker used. LSHIY is now a live Adversary Infrastructure campaign. The next tenant that range touches blocks it at sign-in, whether or not its MFA policy has a gap.

1337 Services GmbH: ten weeks of token replay. Between July and September, an attacker captured sessions through AiTM relays and replayed the stolen tokens from a German hosting provider's 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range. We responded at 79 organizations: 497 successful sign-ins against more than 200,000 failed attempts. The operator rotated through six addresses in that range, one after another, with quiet periods between phases. A block written for one address did nothing against the next. Microsoft flagged them individually. Range-level blocking, maintained by Huntress and updated as the attacker moves, is built for exactly this pattern.

In both cases, the first tenants hit paid the price of cleanup: rogue devices, wiped MFA methods, hidden inbox rules, a payroll email sent to an outside CPA. With Adversary Infrastructure, the next tenant never gets that far.

Where Managed ISPM fits

If you're wondering why Conditional Access blocks live in ITDR when Managed ISPM already manages Conditional Access, here's the clean answer.

ISPM is posture. It deploys broad, durable controls that close whole classes of attack: block device code flow, restrict legacy auth and ROPC, require MFA for all apps. These controls aren't aimed at any one adversary. They're the baseline, and they stay in place. Every policy runs in Learning Mode for 14 days first, so nothing breaks.

Adversary Infrastructure is response. It's narrowly scoped to the exact IP ranges behind incidents the SOC has already reported. It changes as campaigns rotate. Every block fires an incident report. Blocking device code flow is an ISPM policy. Going after Railway is an ITDR policy. Both are Conditional Access, doing different jobs.

They're also better together. ISPM built the plumbing and the expertise to deploy Conditional Access across thousands of tenants without locking anyone out. That's what let us turn the Railway response into a product at all. Posture closes the door. Response catches whoever's still trying the handle.

Already using Managed ITDR? Turn Adversary Infrastructure on to unlock this new protection

Adversary Infrastructure is live in Managed ITDR for Microsoft 365 starting today, November 5.

Existing ITDR partners are opted out by default and can turn it on from the ITDR settings page. Partners onboarding from today forward are opted in by default. Eligible tenants need Entra ID P1 or P2 (Business Premium, or E3 with P1, and up), Security Defaults off, and a healthy, fully onboarded tenant in Huntress.

You must be opted in to be protected, and every tenant you opt in strengthens the herd.

Want the full story? Join me, Rich Mozeleski, and Matt Anderson on November 19 for the livestream Herd Immunity for Microsoft 365: How We Stop Attacks at Sign-In. We'll walk through the campaigns, the nomination gate, and what's coming next.

Ready to try out Adversary Infrastructure in Managed ITDR? Start your free, 14-day trial of Managed ITDR today.

articles.title: Gangsters, Money Trails, and Wuffy | Huntress
articles.context: " - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter
articles.full_text:
Your kids spend a month begging for an AI toy dog they found online. At $30, marked down 70% from $100, it feels cheap enough to risk, and you finally cave. You know online orders like this can go sideways, but the worst-case scenario is a piece of junk and a few disappointed kids, right?

The dog arrives, and it's basically a battery-operated stuffed animal with no AI inside. You mutter a few curse words under your breath and write it off. What you never see is that your $30 went to one of more than 250 near-identical websites in the same cybercrime network.

Mastercard scam investigators ordered the same dog, aka Wuffy, and followed the money trail. The online store looked legit, with a 4.7-star rating and customer support that answered fast and in detail. But the payment record showed a company headquartered in Lithuania while the site listed a US address, and the store had 250 look-alikes that all carried a 4.7-star rating and a 70% discount. Mastercard's analysis tied an estimated $50 million a year in transactions to the network, and the full scale was likely larger.

Why nobody chases a $30 charge

Victims see the loss, but the trail behind it, who got paid and what that money funded next, stays hidden. A scam like Wuffy is built to keep it that way.

According to Ann Johnson, Mastercard's Executive Vice President of Security Solutions, scammers like credit cards because the loss lands on someone else. When a store turns out to be a scam, the bank covers the loss. Scammers rarely have to pay any of it back, and they know it. So they keep prices reasonable on purpose. They list a $100 "regular" price, so $30 feels like a Black Friday deal. They count on buyers to write off a $30 charge, since fighting it costs more time and money than it's worth.

Now multiply that across more than 250 websites. Each charge looks too small to chase, and only someone who connects the dots across all of them sees the full scale.

For the cybercriminal, a convincing cover story and a price nobody pushes back on add up to steady money with little risk. For you, it's a $30 annoyance that's easy to forget.

Where a $40 million ransom really goes

The criminals behind Wuffy hid in plain sight, making small sales incrementally through a legit-looking store and normal payment systems.

Ransomware has the opposite problem. You're the ransomware gang, and the victim just paid, which leaves you holding millions in traceable crypto. No mainstream exchange will take that much without asking questions, so you need someone who can clean it.

Investigative journalist Geoff White, who covers organized crime and technology, tells the story of one reported $40 million ransom paid by CNA Financial, a US financial firm. As he tells it, Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA), in an investigation called Operation Destabilise, followed the money and traced chunks of it to accounts it links to Ekaterina Zhdanova, a Russian socialite.

"CNA Financial's daily revenues are apparently $38 million. It's a massive amount of money. You can't go to Coinbase or Kraken with that huge quantity of money and expect them not to ask a lot of questions. So the hackers were looking for somewhere else to put that money." - Geoff White, author and investigative journalist

Zhdanova reportedly tried Garantex first, a sanctioned Russian exchange, which only made the crypto hotter. Then she turned to UK drug gangs. The NCA says she offered them a swap: their cash for her crypto. The gangs wanted to unload bulky, vulnerable piles of cash, and crypto could cross borders to buy more product.

"Where does the money from ransomware go? Suddenly you expand out into this massive world connecting all these different networks, not just criminal, but illicit and state-level." - Geoff White

The money trail keeps branching. When Russia invaded Ukraine, Russians with frozen money wanted funds in the UK to buy property or pay school fees. Reportedly, they paid Zhdanova in rubles, and she freed up the same amount in cash in the UK.

The NCA says another branch was tied to the Russian government's efforts to move money into the UK to fund spy rings. Police raided a guest house and found surveillance gear, including a Minion toy with a hidden camera. Six people were convicted, and the NCA says Zhdanova sat at the heart of the funding.

The bottom line is that a company that pays a ransom has no way to know where the money will end up, and neither does anyone who pays $30 for a toy dog.

We can all cut off the money trail

Criminals watch their margins closely, so every bit of friction helps, whether you're protecting your own card or your company's accounts.

If a deal or request is too good to be true, it is. Don't share your information. Take your business elsewhere, to retailers you trust.

If someone contacts you claiming to be your bank or a trusted vendor, stop and verify through a number or website you already know, like the one on the back of your card. Spoofed phone numbers are common, and a link a caller sends can be one digit off.

Talk about scams at home and work, especially with younger family members and colleagues, whose sense of what's private online may differ from yours.

Ready to start following the money trail? Watch the full _declassified episode.

articles.title: Threat Hunting: What It Is, How It Works, & Why It Matters
articles.context: threat intelligence Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for...
articles.full_text:
Most security tools catch what they already know: known signatures, known patterns, known behaviors.

The threats that do the most damage don't match anything in the rulebook. They show up with stolen credentials, built-in Windows tools, and quiet moves that look like a normal Tuesday. Yet in our 2025 cybercrime survey, 57% of IT professionals said they're very confident their defenses can catch an advanced attack that doesn't rely on malware signatures. Confidence is nice. Evidence is better.

Threat hunting closes that gap. Here's how.

What is threat hunting?

Threat hunting is the proactive search across networks and endpoints for signs of malicious activity that traditional security defenses missed. Instead of waiting for an alert, analysts assume an attacker could already be inside and go looking for proof. That's what sets cyber threat hunting apart: it starts with a question, not an alert.

Reactive detection waits for a tool to fire, and a tool only fires if someone already wrote the rule. Proactive threat hunting asks, "If an attacker were in here, what would they have touched?" and goes looking before the threat goes down. Think of it as spotting the smoke before the fire, catching early indicators of compromise (IOCs) before they become full-blown incidents.

Every hunt aims to find overlooked activity, cut attacker dwell time, sharpen detection rules, and share intel. So how does it work? A hunter builds a hypothesis, searches telemetry for evidence, and turns what they find into a detection so the next attempt gets caught automatically.

Threat hunting vs. threat detection vs. threat intelligence

Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for what both missed. They feed each other: intel gives hunters hypotheses, and hunts produce new detections.

Threat hunting

Threat detection

Threat intelligence

Main goal

Find hidden, unknown threats that bypassed automated defenses

Identify known malicious activity and generate alerts

Give context on external and emerging threats to inform defenses

Approach

Proactive, human-driven

Reactive, automated

Analytical, research-based

Input/triggers

Hypotheses, threat intel reports, or hunches based on internal context, plus low-priority alerts

Rules, signatures, and known indicators

Raw data, OSINT, dark web, vendor feeds, internal hunting findings

Output

New detection rules and new threat intelligence

Security alerts, incident creation

Actionable reports and feeds

Timing

Periodic or continuous

Real-time or near real-time

Continuous collection and analysis

Key tools

SIEM querying, EDR, network analysis tools, custom scripts

SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, antivirus

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs), OSINT tools, feeds, databases

Primary trigger

Hypothesis-driven

Alert-driven

Research-driven

Typical data sources

EDR and SIEM telemetry

OSINT and threat feeds

Who typically does it

Dedicated threat hunter

SOC analyst

Threat intel analyst

Types of threat hunting

Every hunt falls into one of two types of threat hunting.

Structured threat hunting works from clear hypotheses and well-defined procedures, which keeps it consistent, repeatable, and scalable. Hunters know which tactic, technique, or procedure (TTP) they're after and roughly where to look.

Unstructured threat hunting is guided by curiosity, with no strict guidelines. It's data science applied to security, and it matters because advanced attackers often use never-before-seen techniques that slip past known TTPs. It takes senior-level knowledge to pull off.

Threat hunting methodologies

Structured and unstructured describe how a hunt runs. Threat hunting methodologies describe where it starts. Each uses different threat hunting techniques to reach a testable hypothesis, so the right threat hunting methodology depends on what you've got to work with.

Intelligence-driven hunts

A structured approach that starts with collected intel: file names, hashes, IPs, campaigns, IOCs, email addresses, domains. Hunters form hypotheses and test them internally.

Data-driven hunts

These unstructured hunts start with your own data, like low-priority alerts, detections, or aggregated analytics. None of it is a smoking gun, but it gives hunters a starting point for a hypothesis.

Knowledge-driven hunts

These rely on what hunters know about available data sets, your network, and adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK help them build hypotheses around techniques seen in the wild.

Hybrid hunts

Hybrid hunts combine two or more methodologies. If your data shows odd events on endpoints and intel suggests they match an active campaign, that's a sharper hypothesis than either source gives alone.

The threat hunting process

Good hunts aren't random searches. The cyber threat hunting process for a structured hunt follows three phases.

Planning phase

Gather intelligence. Hunters study risk areas, historical data, and outside sources like open-source intelligence to spot patterns worth chasing.

Build a hypothesis. Hunters make an educated guess about which threat actors, tactics, and techniques might be in play. That hypothesis becomes the north star for the whole hunt.

Identify data sources. With a hypothesis in hand, hunters determine where the evidence would live: system logs, network traffic, endpoint telemetry.

Execution phase

Query the data. Hunters scrutinize data by querying databases, analyzing logs, and doing forensic work.

Follow TTPs and behavioral patterns. Hunters chase breadcrumbs that line up with the hypothesis. Behavior beats indicators here: attackers can swap a file hash in seconds, but they can't easily change how they work, which is why living off the land binaries (LOLBins) show up in so many hunts.

Test and refine. The aim is to prove or disprove the hypothesis, refining the hunt and forming new hypotheses as new information comes in.

Reporting phase

This is where the threat hunting life cycle pays off, because every hunt feeds the next one.

Distill findings. Hunters document what they found, even when the hypothesis didn't pan out.

Create detections. Patterns inform detection rules that catch the activity automatically. If the hunt turned up an active attacker, your incident response plan takes over.

Improve the process. Hunting is iterative, so feed what you learned into the next hunt.

Threat hunting best practices

These seven threat hunting best practices keep your hunts sharp.

Know your environment. You can't spot abnormal if you don't know normal, and good cyber hygiene makes that baseline cleaner.

Use threat intelligence. Feed current intel into your hypotheses so you're hunting what attackers do now.

Keep learning. Threats evolve, so continuous training isn't optional.

Build an adversarial mindset. Be curious and skeptical, and assume breach.

Develop diverse skills. Hunting takes analytical, forensic, and scripting chops (more in the FAQs).

Set aside dedicated time. Hunting should be scheduled, not something analysts only do when they're free.

Automate successful hunts. This one's our favorite: Hunt once, detect forever. When a query finds a real threat, turn it into an automated detection rule in your SIEM (security information event management) or EDR (endpoint detection and response) solution right away. Next time that behavior shows up, your tools catch it automatically, and your hunter gets to chase the next unknown.

Threat hunting tools

You can't hunt what you can't see. A threat hunting platform pulls telemetry, search, and context into one place so hunters can test hypotheses fast. Most hunts use three kinds of tools.

SIEM. A SIEM centralizes logs and alerts from across your environment. In a hunt, that gives hunters one place to query across endpoints, identity, and network traffic, and it's where successful hunts become detection rules. That's why threat hunting SIEM workflows anchor most mature programs.

EDR. EDR threat hunting starts with endpoint telemetry like process launches, file changes, and network connections, so hunters can spot a trusted admin tool launching from a strange folder. With Managed EDR, expert analysts do the watching for you, and pairing it with identity coverage through unified EDR and ITDR keeps attackers from slipping between the endpoint and the account.

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs). TIPs aggregate threat data from multiple sources. For hunters, that's a steady supply of fresh hypotheses without reading a hundred feeds, and it keeps intel tied to the hunt instead of buried in a PDF.

Why threat hunting matters

Automated tools can't out-think a human adversary. Machine learning is great at speed and known patterns, but a person still has to decide what's suspicious. Modern attackers know that, and they actively probe for blind spots in automated detection.

With human-powered threat hunting, a trained eye picks up on odd behavior no rule was written for, and every hunt makes your automated tools more accurate. The payoff is finding unknown threats early: before ransomware gets deployed, before malware spreads, before anyone's weekend goes up in smoke.

Want to see it in practice? Watch the video below.

How Huntress supports threat hunting

The most effective threat hunting pairs human analyst expertise with the right tooling layer. Without centralized visibility, hunters are working blind, leaving gaps for attackers.

That's where Huntress Managed SIEM comes in. It gives you the data foundation for every phase of the hunt:

Smart Filtering technology cuts the noise so analysts focus on real signals.

Centralized log management puts the data you need in one place for planning, execution, and reporting.

24/7 SOC coverage means the hunt doesn't stop when your internal team goes offline.

Attackers don't clock out at five. Your hunt shouldn't either. Start a free trial or request a demo and see what's hiding in your logs. Happy hunting.

FAQs

What is the main objective of threat hunting?

The main objective of threat hunting is to proactively search for and identify hidden, unknown malicious activity that slips past existing automated security controls and detection systems.

What is the difference between SOC and threat hunting?

The security operations center (SOC) is the central, general-purpose team responsible for monitoring, detecting, analyzing, and responding to known security incidents reactively. Threat hunting is the human-driven, proactive discipline within the SOC focused on searching for unknown and persistent threats that have evaded the standard automated SOC tools.

What are four main types of threats?

Cyber threats are usually divided into four main types: malware, social engineering, network attacks, and application or web attacks.

articles.title: Reports of SIEM's Death Have Been Greatly Exaggerated
articles.context: Lean on a partner for the threats that look bad anywhere, and build your own detections for the things only your team would know are off
articles.full_text:
There's a phrase I keep hearing in cyber circles lately, at in-person conferences, on LinkedIn, pretty much everywhere:

"SIEM is dead."

I get why it's catchy. But SIEM has died more times than a soap opera villain, and it keeps showing up for next season. Before SIEM, it was the perimeter that was dead. Then antivirus. Then passwords. (Passkeys are coming for them, but plenty are still living on sticky notes under keyboards.)

Here's where I land: the way a lot of companies have been buying and feeding their SIEM deserves to go away. SIEM itself doesn't. So before anyone orders flowers, let's look at what's actually changing.

Follow the money (and the marketing)

There's so much cybersecurity marketing out there that it's hard to tell which tools and controls matter against today's threats. Every booth on the expo floor has "AI" printed on it somewhere. Some of it is impressive. Some of it is a chatbot wearing a trench coat.

"X is dead" is about the oldest trick in the marketing book. If the old category is dead, you'd better buy the new one. It makes for a great keynote slide. It also skips the question I'd want answered first: what was the old thing doing for us, and do we still need that done?

For SIEM, the job was visibility across the environment, catching attackers, running investigations, and keeping records for compliance. Attackers are still here. So are auditors. The open question is whether there's a smarter way to do it.

The "send it all" era

For years, the big legacy players (think Splunk and QRadar) priced on how much data you ingested and how much you stored. That model let them charge what they charged.

And the advice that came with it was always the same: send everything. Firewall logs, DNS queries, DHCP renewals, every time a printer had feelings. Get it all in, and figure out what's useful later.

Later almost never came. What came instead was a giant bill, a pile of alerts nobody had time for, and a very expensive junk drawer.

If your vendor makes more money every time you send another log, of course they'll tell you to send more.

The market has caught on. Cisco bought Splunk, and IBM sold its QRadar SaaS business to Palo Alto Networks. When the biggest names in a category start changing hands, something is shifting.

Enter the AI-native challengers

That market shake-up opened the door for a wave of AI-native SIEMs and security data lakes. The newest pitch I keep hearing goes something like:

"Why store everything yourself? Leave the logs where they are. Our AI will call your sources' APIs, pull what it needs on demand, and only keep the signals that matter."

I'll be fair. That sounds great, and some of the thinking behind it is smart. Nobody enjoys paying to store terabytes of noise, and using AI to pick out signal is a useful idea.

The problem is the bill.

You swapped a storage bill for a token bill

When AI is querying everything on demand, you're still paying. You've just moved the cost from storage to compute, specifically the tokens it takes to pull, parse, and reason over that data each time. During an active incident, when you're firing off question after question, that meter moves fast. It's like cutting the cable bill and then signing up for nine streaming services.

Also, tokens right now are about as cheap and subsidized as they'll ever be. AI providers are pricing to win market share, and that won't last.

We've been here before: Moving everything to the cloud was going to save us all a fortune, remember? For plenty of companies it did, right up until the egress fees and surprise invoices showed up and someone had to go hire a FinOps team. Prices settled at their real level. I expect AI inference to follow a similar path.

Cost isn't the only catch, either:

Retention: If the source system only keeps 30 days of logs, then so do you, which hurts when you find out about a breach on day 45.

Availability: Your investigations depend on someone else's API being up and free of rate limits, usually at the exact moment you need answers.

Compliance: Telling an auditor or your cyber insurance carrier "we can go fetch it if we need it" makes for a tough conversation.

A better approach: store what matters, keep what you're required to keep

In my opinion, the best way to get real security value out of logs sits somewhere between hoarding everything and storing nothing. Only store the logs that matter.

That's how we approach it at Huntress. Our smart filtering removes logs that aren't security relevant before they ever hit storage, so you're paying for signal and not chatter. The logs that drive detections and investigations stick around.

Filtering doesn't mean ignoring compliance. If HIPAA, PCI DSS, CMMC, or your cyber insurance policy says you need certain records for a certain amount of time, keep them. Those logs might not catch an attacker in real time, but after an incident they're how you show you did things right.

When I talk with teams about this, I usually suggest running every log source through a simple filter:

Detect: Does this help us spot or investigate a threat? Keep it.

Prove: Does a regulation, auditor, or insurer require it? Keep it.

Drop: Neither? Drop it. Nobody's going to miss the printer logs.

The bill shrinks, sure. The bigger win is fewer false positives, faster investigations, and analysts who spend their day hunting threats rather than scrolling past junk.

So where does AI belong?

AI isn't the bad guy here. It absolutely has a place in a modern SIEM. What I care about is whether it's running on every log, all the time, with the meter spinning, or whether someone decided where it actually helps.

Once you've filtered down to security-relevant data, AI gets a lot more useful and a lot cheaper, because it has far less to dig through.

Correlation is where I think it shines most. A VPN login from a country the user has never been to is interesting on its own. Now add an encoded PowerShell command running on a server that same account touched ten minutes later, and then a new inbox rule in their Microsoft 365 account forwarding mail to an outside address. Separately those are three data points. Together they're an incident. Pulling EDR and ITDR telemetry together with the logs coming in from across the rest of IT, and lining it all up into one timeline, is a great job for AI.

It also helps with the grunt work of an investigation, like summarizing what a user did in the last 24 hours instead of handing an analyst 4,000 raw log lines. It can add context during triage, such as whether an IP has a bad reputation or whether this process normally runs on this host. And it can write up findings in plain English for the people who don't speak fluent ES|QL, which is most of leadership and every auditor I've met.

In every one of those cases, AI shows up after the filtering, at a specific point where it helps someone make a better call. Detections and real SOC analysts still decide whether something is malicious. That control is what keeps things predictable. You know where AI is being used, so you have a decent idea what it'll cost, and it isn't dreaming up alerts out of nowhere, which keeps false positives down.

Who owns what? The shared responsibility nobody puts on the sales slide

SIEM is one piece of the bigger SecOps picture, alongside EDR, identity threat detection, security awareness training, backups, and an incident response plan you've hopefully tested at least once. So when you're figuring out what to run in house and what to hand to a partner, keep in mind that even with a managed SIEM, some of the work stays with you.

Cloud providers figured this out years ago. AWS will lock down the data center, but if you leave an S3 bucket open to the internet, that one's on you. Managed SIEM works the same way.

What your partner should handle

Some activity looks malicious in pretty much any network. Credential stuffing. A user getting hammered with MFA prompts until they finally tap "approve." Shadow copies getting wiped. Someone dumping credentials out of memory with Mimikatz.

This is where you should be able to fully lean on a partner like Huntress. Our SOC sees attacker tradecraft across hundreds of thousands of environments, so when a new technique or IOC pops up in one place, we go looking for it everywhere else. One internal team can't get that view on its own. Detection engineering, tuning, 24/7 triage, and active remediation (isolating hosts, killing sessions, locking accounts, cleaning up persistence) are all things we own, across endpoint, identity, and SIEM. We don't just hand you a pile of alerts.

What only you can catch

Then there's the stuff that could be totally fine or a huge red flag, and the only way to know is whether your team expected it.

A remote access tool you didn't approve. ScreenConnect showing up on a workstation could be your help desk. It could also be an attacker, or a "helpful" vendor, setting up shop. Only you know which RMM tools are sanctioned in your environment.

A new admin account. Was that new domain admin part of a change ticket, or did it just appear on a Friday afternoon?

An off-hours login to a critical system. For one company that's the overnight batch job. For another it's the first sign someone has the keys to the ERP.

A service account wandering off its usual path. Service accounts are supposed to run in the background, not log into the VPN from a laptop. If one shows up in your VPN logs, someone may be using its credentials as a side door.

Firewall rule or group policy changes outside a maintenance window. If nobody on your team made the change, someone else did.

Your approved software list, your change calendar, and your maintenance windows live with your team. We can tell you a service account just logged into the VPN. Only you can say whether Jim from IT set that up as a "temporary" workaround three years ago.

That's where your own saved queries and custom detections come in. You know what "weird for us" looks like, so you write the logic, and you decide what to do when it fires. The SIEM gives you the data in one place to do it.

Response is a team sport, too

A partner like Huntress can stop the bleeding and clean up after it. But some calls only you can make. Do you take the production line offline? Notify customers? Loop in legal, the insurer, or HR? Which servers can be isolated on a Tuesday afternoon, and which ones need a phone call first?

Get your own leadership, IT, legal, and HR on the same page before an incident. Decide who owns which calls, who gets the phone call, and which actions are pre-approved. With Huntress, you choose where and how we respond in your environment, so those decisions carry straight through to how we act. Revisit them after every incident. Trust me, you don't want to be figuring out who's allowed to disable the CEO's account at 2 a.m.

The partnerships I've seen work best aren't "set it and forget it." It's more like "set it, tell us what matters, and we'll both sleep better."

So, is SIEM dead?

Nope. If there's one thing I'd want you to take away, it's to be intentional.

Be intentional about what you store. Keep the logs that help you detect and the ones that help you prove, and drop the rest. Be intentional about where you use AI. Point it at the spots where it sharpens the picture, like tying endpoint, identity, and log data together, instead of running it everywhere because you can. And be intentional about who's watching for what. Lean on a partner for the threats that look bad anywhere, and build your own detections for the things only your team would know are off.

The question I'd ask isn't whether SIEM is dead. It's whether yours is earning its keep.

Want to see what a SIEM looks like when it only keeps what matters? See Huntress Managed SIEM in action.

articles.title: Managed for Malice: How Attackers Turn MDM into Remote Access
articles.context: Background Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks
articles.full_text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Lindsey Welch, Anton Ovrutsky, and Harlan Carvey for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Huntress has observed several incidents recently where threat actors have leveraged mobile device management (MDM) applications to carry out attacks. In these cases, legitimate management tools are being weaponized for malicious purposes, as opposed to threat actors taking advantage of inherent weaknesses in the applications themselves, such as vulnerabilities.

MDM platforms are legitimate tools that organizations use to manage employee laptops, phones, and other devices. These tools help IT teams to enroll and configure company devices remotely, enforce security policies, and deploy approved applications. However, these applications' centralized control and trusted level of access can create an entry point for threat actors if the tools are misused.

These incidents often begin with social engineering—users falling subject to business-themed lures that arrive through messaging applications and email. While not a definitive list of MDMs that could be used in such attacks, we have seen threat actors recently using well-known applications from Hexnode and Rippling.

Once registered with the MDM application, the attacker gains a trusted and privileged management path on the system. In both cases described here, Huntress observed the threat actors installing unauthorized RMM (remote monitoring and management) tools in order to further their attacks.

Mystery of the reappearing ScreenConnect

Imagine receiving an alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation. Naturally, given the severity of such an alert, you prioritize it and remove the ScreenConnect agent immediately. However, several hours later, you receive another alert—same unauthorized installation. Something's clearly going on behind the scenes.

A recurring ScreenConnect installation is the first clue that this is more than an isolated, rogue RMM deployment. If both installations connected to the same destination relay, this would suggest the same threat actor was involved both times.

So how are they managing to get back in after being removed once?

We observed this activity in a recent incident, where two Huntress alerts for unauthorized ScreenConnect activity on the same device, separated by several hours, connected to the same relay.

As it happened, a threat actor had previously managed to install an MDM client from Hexnode on the system that ScreenConnect kept appearing on. Removing the RMM did little to deter them. They simply staged and installed the RMM software again.

The attack began with a phishing email. The target received several emails with proposal-related subjects like "ATTN: Official Invitation to Submit Proposal" and "Review Required" that mentioned an organization that the target likely had a business relationship with.

Clicking a link contained within the email downloaded a file from https://webdocusign.viewportal[.]es/Windows/download/index.php

which was saved to the Microsoft Edge temporary downloads folder as eD0cuSign_Installer.msi.

While the file had been named to mimic a DocuSign installer, it actually contained an installation package for a Hexnode MDM, a legitimate device management application. The package included Hexnode Gateway, the Hexnode agent, and supporting PostgreSQL components, all of which were installed on the system.

Figure 1: Execution of the Hexnode MSI, designed to resemble a (fake) DocuSign installer.

The threat actor followed up by installing ScreenConnect shortly thereafter and connecting to the attacker-controlled relay, relay.bobdthjau[.]com:8041. This resulted in a Huntress alert for an unauthorized ScreenConnect installation, and the MSP removed the RMM from the compromised computer shortly thereafter.

However, several hours later another instance of ScreenConnect was installed and reconnected to the relay. This triggered another alert, which led Huntress to isolate the endpoint, and a thorough remediation began.

Enrollment from a link

Not all incidents involve phishing techniques that trick a user into running an MSI installer. In another instance, a receptionist opened an email titled "Re: Tax Planning and Preparation Inquiry." The email included a link to what appeared to be a Microsoft Teams meeting invitation.

Clicking the link brought the target to a page titled "Calendar." While the site was taken down shortly after the attempt, it likely impersonated a Teams scheduling calendar. This page redirected to a .php file that appears to have helped facilitate enrollment into an attacker-controlled Rippling MDM tenant. All three links resided on the following domain (see the IoCs section for full URLs):

https://teams-microsoftcom5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592.kiratham[.]com

About a minute after clicking the link, a Rippling enrollment registry key appeared on the compromised system, which is consistent with registration in the MDM platform. An installation MSI for the Rippling agent was subsequently downloaded to C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\mdm\{GUID}.msi. The agent was then installed with SYSTEM-level permissions as C:\Rippling\daemon.exe.

Further investigation by Huntress determined that this activity originated from the online Rippling management agent, suggesting that the threat actor had previously created an account to carry out the attack.

Approximately 35 minutes after installation, the attackers used the MDM to stage and run a ScreenConnect installer as SYSTEM, connecting back to an attacker-controlled domain relay.pronconetydesire[.]online:8041, triggering a Huntress alert for a malicious ScreenConnect instance.

Tradecraft patterns & motivations

These instances, and the abuse of MDM applications in general, highlights a frustrating situation for security practitioners. The challenge is that more tools designed to help organizations manage endpoints are becoming mechanisms to compromise them. Similar to the illegitimate use of RMMs, this further complicates what we can safely consider trusted software, because reputation alone is just not sufficient to determine intent. Neither Hexnode nor Rippling are at fault here—users are simply being socially engineered into installing their software.

So where does this leave us? MDM enrollment should be treated as security-sensitive activity as opposed to a routine administrative task. An unexpected enrollment can establish persistence, provide a privileged deployment path, and allow an attacker to introduce additional tooling without relying on conspicuous payloads like known malware.

These incidents also demonstrate how detection cannot treat RMM installation as an isolated event. While the RMM client, and its subsequent activity, may have been the most visible part of the intrusion, removing it does not remove the unauthorized management architecture that delivered it.

The sequence of events observed makes for a stronger signal—social engineering -> a new MDM enrollment -> RMM installation -> outbound communication with an unfamiliar relay. Because the chain can vary, correlation across identity, MDM, endpoint, and network telemetry is our best hope in providing the resiliency needed to defend against these attacks.

Mitigation Guidance

Organizations can reduce the risk faced by these techniques by controlling both the enrollment path and the applications that MDM platforms are allowed to deploy.

Maintain an inventory of authorized MDM products, tenants, agents, and RMM instances. Treat any unexpected enrollment, management agent, or RMM instance as a security event.

Train users to verify unexpected meeting, document-signing, and proposal-review requests. Email and web controls should also scrutinize business-themed lures.

If a compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint, remove the endpoint from the unauthorized MDM tenant, disable attacker-created accounts, revoke active sessions or tokens, reset affected credentials, and reimage the endpoint if its integrity cannot be confirmed.

Delivery URL for the fake DocuSign/proposal installer in the Hexnode case.
