articles.title: Attack Reduction in Huntress Managed ESPM: Disrupting ClickFix
articles.context: Introducing Attack Reduction Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on,...
articles.full_text:
Mandy was stuck at an airport with a few hours to kill. She decided to get her nails done, so she found a spa listed on the airport's website and clicked through. It looked like the spa's real website, on a normal domain with HTTPS, and Chrome showed no warnings.

Then a CAPTCHA popped up. Nothing too unusual there. It asked for a few "verification steps" to ensure she was a human user:

Press and hold Windows key + R

In the verification window, press Ctrl + V

Press Enter

An example ClickFix attack where a user is told to press "Windows Key + R" and paste a command into the Run dialog that opens.

But this simple sequence of hotkeys actually opens the Windows Run dialog, and in this case, would have pasted a malicious PowerShell command that the webpage quietly copied to the clipboard. (The Windows Run dialog is a small box that lets you type a command or program name and run it right away.)

If Mandy pressed Enter, the command would have downloaded and run a file from the internet. That file sets up persistence through a registry key, installs a remote access trojan, and steals the browser's saved passwords, cookies, and credit card details.

This is not a hypothetical example. This actually happened to a Huntress employee (name changed for privacy). Thankfully, she realized what was going on and didn't get pwned. A LOT of people aren't so lucky. So, this post is about one simple idea: what if "Windows key + R" didn't open anything at all?

What is ClickFix, and why is it everywhere?

ClickFix is a simple social engineering attack that tricks users into running malicious commands they don't understand. It often employs messaging related to fixing a problem, hence the name "ClickFix."

It also works very well. Our 2026 Cyber Threat Report linked ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA scams to over half of all malware loader activity. In our own SOC, ClickFix-style Run dialog attacks now account for 31% of EDR SOC signals.

The lures keep changing: fake Windows Update screens, fake Docker ads, compromised small-business websites, and now malicious AI chatbots. But the classic version almost always ends the same way, with Windows key + R.

Most of your users should never open the Run dialog

Here's what makes this so frustrating. The Run dialog is a power-user shortcut. IT folks love it. Most employees have never opened it on purpose and wouldn't know what to type into it if they did.

We've seen this play out in the data. Across organizations in ESPM Early Access, it's common to see 90% or more of users who never use the Run dialog at all. Which is why they don't recognize the commands they are pasting in as being a problem.

Run dialog box on Windows in which a user has pasted a malicious command, unwittingly copied from a ClickFix attack.

That's a big gap. A feature almost nobody needs is the starting point for nearly a third of what our EDR SOC investigates. Detection still matters, and Huntress Managed EDR's Attack Disruption engine can kill many ClickFix chains in under a second. But when the attack depends on a feature your users don't need, the simplest fix is to turn that feature off. If only there was an easy way to do that…Oh, wait, now there is!

Introducing Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on, starting with "Windows key + R". That fits what ESPM is built to do: harden your endpoints before an attack ever starts.

ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard

We're starting with the Run dialog, because that's where ClickFix starts. More controls are coming:

Available now: Blocking the Run dialog for users who don't need it to disrupt "Windows key + R" attacks.

Planned: Command Prompt restrictions for users who don't use cmd.exe.

Planned: Interactive PowerShell restrictions for users who don't use it.

Planned: Windows Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that stop Office, script, and email apps from launching or injecting payloads.

Planned: Blocking HTML applications (mshta) for users who don't use them.

How Attack Reduction works

The hard part of turning off a Windows feature isn't flipping the switch. It's knowing who will be affected and not breaking legitimate workflows. Attack Reduction is designed with the following in mind.

1. See who actually uses the Run dialog

Once ESPM is on, Attack Reduction collects each user's Run dialog history and builds a baseline. On the Attack Reduction dashboard, you can see which users rely on the Run dialog and which never touch it, across your whole account or one organization at a time. You'll know exactly who would be affected before anything changes.

The dashboard also flags commands in a user's Run history that look like ClickFix. Windows doesn't record when those commands ran, so treat them as a reason to investigate rather than proof of an active attack.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and how many users are utilizing the Run dialog per week.

2. Turn on blocking

When you're ready, turn on blocking at the account or organization level. Attack Reduction then turns off the "Windows key + R" shortcut for users who don't need it. Users who rely on the Run dialog can keep it, and you can switch any user between allowed and blocked at any time.

3. Users get a clear message, not a mystery

If a blocked user presses Windows key + R, nothing runs. Instead, they see a pop-up explaining that the action was blocked for security reasons and asking them to contact their IT support team or take Security Awareness Training. Either way, the attack stops, and a confused user gets a quick security lesson.

4. You get a record of what they almost ran

When a blocked user presses Windows key + R, Attack Reduction also captures what was on their clipboard. If someone was about to paste a malicious command, you'll have it on record, which helps you spot users who are being targeted and follow up.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and a list of blocked attempts by users to utilize the Run dialog.

What Attack Reduction doesn't do

We want to be clear about the limits here, because ClickFix is a moving target.

Blocking the Run dialog disrupts the most common version of ClickFix. It doesn't stop every one. Attackers can, and already do, tell users to paste commands into File Explorer's address bar, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell instead.

That's why the Run dialog is the first step, not the last one. Every path we close makes the attack harder to pull off, and the planned Command Prompt and PowerShell controls are aimed at exactly those next moves. Attack Reduction also works best alongside the rest of your defenses: Managed EDR to catch what gets through, and Managed SAT so users know a real CAPTCHA will never ask them to paste a command.

Get started with Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access for existing Huntress partners and customers.

Not in ESPM Early Access yet? Click the ESPM icon in the left-hand menu of your Huntress portal to enroll. Then let Attack Reduction collect a baseline so you can see which users actually need the Run dialog before flipping on Blocking.

As Early Access partners put this capability to work, their feedback will decide which Windows features we tackle next and how we build those controls.

Have ideas or requests? Share them at feedback.huntress.com/espm. And stay tuned. There's a lot more coming to Managed ESPM.

articles.title: Introducing ITDR Lookback: Find Out Who Was in Your Microsoft 365 Tenant Before You Were
articles.context: Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants
articles.full_text:
Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants. Lookback automatically examines up to 180 days of login history to uncover evidence of compromise before Huntress connected. When a compromise is still active, our Security Operations Center (SOC) investigates and revokes the identity's active sessions.

Onboarding a Microsoft 365 tenant feels like a fresh start. You go through your checklist, and a successful connection tells you monitoring has started. But it doesn't tell you if an attacker got there first. Your first day protecting a tenant might be an attacker's twenty-seventh day inside.

That's what Lookback seeks to solve. You get a clearer picture of the tenant you've inherited, plus defenders who act on what they find. And yes, that includes trial tenants.

Six months of login history. A much stronger start.

Lookback runs once, automatically, when a Microsoft 365 tenant finishes onboarding to Managed ITDR. There's nothing extra to configure and no separate scan to remember to launch.

Huntress Managed ITDR's new Lookback feature is generally available, bringing up to 180 days of Microsoft 365 login history into the hunt for existing compromises.

Lookback applies Huntress's full set of Unwanted Access detections to the tenant's available Microsoft 365 login history, looking back up to 180 days. That includes detections for credential theft, token theft, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, suspicious browsers, and datacenter logins.

Here's the tricky part: evidence of an old compromise doesn't necessarily mean an attacker still has access. Someone may have already reset the password or revoked the compromised sessions. Treating every historical finding as a fresh emergency would make onboarding pretty miserable.

Lookback separates findings based on whether the compromise is still active:

Active compromises receive a critical Incident Report investigated by the Huntress AI-centric SOC, with the identity's active sessions revoked. This turns historical evidence into a reason to act right away.

Previously remediated compromises appear in the Identity Security Assessment as historical context. They don't trigger a new incident or an unnecessary lockdown for something you've already fixed.

That distinction matters. A raw list of suspicious logins leaves the sorting to you. Lookback does it first, so you can see what happened and which parts still need attention.

What's in the report, and where do you find it?

Lookback adds a dedicated section to the Identity Security Assessment, covering compromises that predate Huntress monitoring. It shows the period reviewed and previously remediated incidents, including affected identities, relevant dates, and observed remediation evidence, such as a password reset or session revocation. The report gives you a documented history you can use in a customer conversation or share with leadership.

That history sits alongside the assessment's existing coverage of identities, Rogue Apps, Shadow Workflows such as malicious inbox rules, Unwanted Access, and SOC findings and containment actions. Active compromises uncovered by Lookback also receive their own Incident Reports.

Lookback is part of onboarding for newly connected Microsoft 365 tenants. The assessment is generated automatically after onboarding and waits for Lookback to finish, so you receive one complete document. Once that historical review is complete, Managed ITDR continues monitoring for new threats with the Huntress SOC behind it.

The attackers who arrived before we did

In Lookback's first two weeks of early testing, Huntress reviewed more than 400 tenants. Among them were three very different organizations with the same unwelcome surprise: an active compromise already in progress.

A title company and a $2 million wire

A device-code phishing attack gave an adversary access three days before the tenant onboarded. The attacker persisted through a rogue Entra device and was watching a $2 million real estate wire transfer. Lookback surfaced the active compromise, which Huntress contained.

For a business moving that kind of money, "let's wait until the attacker does something else" is a lousy security strategy.

A school district with an unwanted administrator

A school district's Global Admin account had been compromised 27 days before onboarding. An unrevoked refresh token and a rogue Azure AD device kept the attacker's access alive, with the privileges to control the tenant. Lookback uncovered the compromise, and Huntress contained it. Twenty-seven days is a long head start. Connecting a new security tool shouldn't give the attacker more time simply because the break-in happened earlier.

An architecture firm turned into a phishing launchpad

An architecture firm onboarded with a nine-day foothold still active. The attack involved a hidden inbox rule and 103 external OneDrive phishing invitations sent in a single scripted second. The compromised account had become infrastructure for targeting other people. Lookback surfaced the compromise, which Huntress contained.

In all three cases, the attack began before onboarding. Looking backward gave our defenders evidence to act on right away, without waiting for an attacker's next move.

Less guesswork for you, more proof for your customers

If you're an MSP, every new client brings a history you didn't write. You still have to explain what you've inherited and what you plan to do about it.

Lookback helps you start that relationship with evidence from the client's own environment. You can show past compromises, distinguish resolved activity from active threats, and explain where Huntress has intervened. The shareable assessment makes that conversation easier, while SOC investigation and containment keep the historical review from becoming another helpdesk project.

Internal IT teams get the same benefit. Whether you've inherited a tenant through an acquisition, a vendor change, or staff turnover, you don't have to become a Microsoft audit log specialist to spot signs of prior compromise.

And if you're evaluating Huntress, your trial includes the same Lookback protection as a paid tenant. You can see what we find in your environment and how we respond to active threats while you're still making your decision.

Looking back is how we keep moving forward

articles.title: ConnectWise (SkyKick) Vendor Credentials Abused in M365 Attacks
articles.context: Update: 10/27/26 @ 2:30PM ET In an October 21 report, Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise credential abuse to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX,...
articles.full_text:
Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Rich Mozeleski, Andrew Brandt, Andrew Kaiser, Dave Kleinatland, and Matt Kiely for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 10/27/26 @ 2:30PM ET

In an October 21 report, Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise credential abuse to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent AI framework, in the attack. We have released a follow-up blog analyzing our own telemetry and how it aligns with these findings.

Update: 10/19/26 @ 1:30 PM ET

This update covers three topics: additional IP addresses circulating in connection with this activity, what we have learned about the attacker's behavior after gaining access, and the art of precision strikes against adversaries.

Additional IP addresses: As more addresses have been shared across the community, we reviewed each against our telemetry. In a review of application sign-ins across more than 10,000 tenants with ConnectWise applications (where we can see those logs), 144.172.64[.]128 and Microsoft-internal ranges are the only addresses that produced application sign-in activity. We did not see application sign-in activity from any of the other addresses listed below, all of which are in the same provider range as 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting). We did see password spray and failed login attempts from some of them. At this time, we do not believe those attempts are related to the application sign-ins described in this post.

IPs and characterizations below:

IP

Description

144.172.64[.]128

Application sign-ins with a vendor credential (primary vector)

144.172.64[.]99

Failed user password spray, concentrated (October 10 to 14)

144.172.64[.]60

A few failed user logins (October 18)

144.172.94[.]243

Broad failed login spray, ongoing, many organizations

What happened after access was gained: Since our last update, Huntress has identified a second tenant with post-compromise activity. Huntress was not deployed on this tenant originally, but we saw service principal sign-in attempts from that tenant to Huntress-protected tenants (from the *.128 IP address). Working proactively with a partner, we were able to get Huntress deployed to this second tenant in order to collect additional telemetry.

In the two tenants with this activity, the post-compromise behavior was fast, scripted, and notably indiscriminate. In both tenants, the post-compromise activities took place within two minutes of each other around 03:45 UTC on October 15. The procedure was the same each time: the application granted itself Global Administrator, then planted a new secret on a small number of other applications in the tenant to keep a foothold. The choice of which applications to backdoor appeared to be random in the two tenants we reviewed. Across the two compromised tenants, the identical grant flow selected two completely different sets of applications. Notably, one application existed in BOTH tenants but was chosen for secret planting in only one of them. In one tenant, the applications that received planted secrets were among the least privileged in the environment, while far more powerful applications sat untouched. The only consistent criteria we can point to is structural: credentials were planted in applications that are registered inside the affected tenant, without regard to what those applications can actually do.

Just as important is what we did not see: The access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, which leave no audit record. In the two tenants we reviewed, we also found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation, or user or policy changes.

Our surgical response: You might be wondering why our response did not include mass disabling the ConnectWise/SkyKick apps across every tenant. Our approach to containment is deliberate, surgical, and evidence-based, and this incident called for a scalpel, not a hammer. We prioritized the tenants with confirmed successful unauthorized sign-ins, and our guidance for everyone else has been to disable the affected apps and check their logs.

When our investigation kicked off, we quickly established a clear picture of the attack window. The malicious application sign-ins were tightly bunched across the morning of October 15 UTC, and the last confirmed successful sign-in we observed with this credential was at 08:44 UTC on October 15. After that, we saw only failed attempts in the tenants where we can see sign-in logs. With evidence in hand that there was no current or repeated activity (in the tenants where we can see sign-in logs), it simply didn't make sense to create a larger-than-necessary blast radius.

This judgment call allowed our experts and agents to focus closely on environments with confirmed unauthorized sign-ins, share what we found with industry partners, and publish guidance for the community.

We believe it's these surgical moments our partners most appreciate and count on when it hits the fan, especially when the wrong decision can disrupt working systems and business productivity as collateral damage.

Update: 10/17/26 @ 5:15 PM ET

**As of October 17 at 5:15 PM ET, ConnectWise has communicated that they have disabled relevant apps.

During further investigations, Huntress identified a second, targeted wave of attempts from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, unsuccessfully targeting a narrow scope of 16 Huntress-protected tenants. These tenants are in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors. Unlike the first wave of activity outlined in our initial blog below, most of these tenants do not rely on any ConnectWise products. In tenants without the relevant ConnectWise service principal, the attempts failed because the application was not present.

For the new target set, the first sweep targeted Graph tokens from the SkyKick app and occurred on October 15 between 09:25:04 and 12:35:50 UTC. Several tenants were hit in bursts during that timeframe. The second sweep hit the same tenants on the same date, between 13:54:39 and 14:20:24 UTC. This sweep appeared to be manual and targeted Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and the Office 365 Management APIs.

In addition to the activity above:

Huntress has identified almost 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the IP address associated with the unauthorized activity (144.172.64[.]128). Over 300 of those succeeded.

While many of these sign-ins were successful, the absence of a service principal in some tenants prevented the threat actor from successfully gaining access to those tenants.

Huntress have also received external reports and tips from outside our fleet describing similar activity in other tenants, including what appears to be hands-on activity. We have not independently verified these reports.

As mentioned in our initial blog, on October 15 the threat actor appears to have used access from the ConnectWise app family to add a credential to a Huntress application in one customer tenant, and to add a credential to another application in the same tenant. The credential on the Huntress application was used to sign in seven times in quick succession. On October 16, Huntress identified and removed the unauthorized credential on our application. We have not seen the application make changes in that tenant's audit log, but Microsoft does not log everything an application reads, so we cannot rule out access to data the application can read there. Huntress is actively reviewing credential activity associated with our applications across partner environments, validating expected access, and investigating suspicious changes.

Notably, the access that led to the credential being added to Huntress and another app came from private Azure IPv6 space, not the IP address associated with the previous sign-ins (144.172.64[.]128). At this time, we advise all ConnectWise users to audit all service principal sign-ins to the apps identified below beginning around 01:00 UTC on October 15 to 02:00 UTC on October 16.

We're strengthening our safeguards with additional monitoring and preventative controls to help detect and respond to unusual activity even faster. We've enabled App Instance Property Lock across all Huntress applications and are enhancing our fleet health and monitoring capabilities to detect modification attempts.

Huntress is continuing to investigate this incident and will update this blog with any further breaking updates.

Update: 10/17/26 @ 10:30 AM ET

After spending the night combing through Azure logs, we have high-confidence that the threat actor has also abused the following M365 applications:

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online (b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519).

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640).

• ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Online (b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb).

At the moment, it does not look like these apps have been disabled by ConnectWise.

When it comes to early exploitation and post-exploitation behaviors, we’ve observed what might be an affinity towards alphabetical targeting (our most interesting victims start with “A”). Although all tenants should be scrutinized, this pattern is worth sharing for prioritization.

If you’ve been impacted with noteworthy tradecraft relating to this SkyKick incident, our research team would love to learn more so we take actions to protect the community. Hit us up at [email protected].

Background

ConnectWise Cloud Backup (Formerly SkyKick) is a cloud-based backup and recovery service built for managed service providers (MSPs) to protect their clients' Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace data. To do that job, the app is granted broad access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data in every tenant it is installed in.

On October 15, the application's identity signed in to customer Microsoft 365 tenants from 144.172.64[.]128, a hosting provider address, and received Microsoft Graph access tokens. This is not how the app normally behaves: legitimate traffic comes from Azure private IP space. As of 19:00 UTC on October 16, Huntress has confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants.

The authentication itself is certain: It comes from Microsoft's own sign-in logs in each tenant. The credential type was a client assertion, which means the credential lives in the vendor's own tenant. Nothing a customer did in their environment could have produced it.

ConnectWise has acknowledged the incident on its website and confirmed the IP is associated with unauthorized activity. Todyl has also reported on this incident.

Figure 1: What the login attempt looks like to an IT admin in the Microsoft Entra Admin Center

Huntress is continuing to monitor this situation closely alongside our security partners; for all updates, please continue to check this blog post.

What Happened

What do we know? The app's credential is in hostile hands. It was used to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants from 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC. The actor moved through tenants in sorted GUID order, a few seconds apart, which points to a script working from a target list.

Who is affected? Any organization with the app installed. The credential works against every tenant the app is consented in, so the actor is not limited to the tenants we have confirmed so far.

How does it work? The attacker authenticates to the app using their own tooling, the same way the backup service does, and gets tokens with the app's existing permissions.

What are the potential repercussions? Because backup and restore both need to read and write data, those permissions are broad. An attacker holding those tokens can read the same mailboxes, files, and directory data the backup service can.

Huntress observations

Here is the timeline of what Huntress has seen from the same infrastructure:

October 13 to 14: Password spraying against four law firm tenants from 144.172.64[.]128. Scripted OAuth2 token requests (User-Agent curl/7.88.1) from datacenter infrastructure. Two accounts were locked out by smart lockout. We saw no successful user sign-ins from this IP in Huntress telemetry.

October 15, from 01:58 UTC: In roughly 50 tenants monitored by Huntress, service principals for ConnectWise's Cloud Management apps (Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft Graph) assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator. The User-Agent on these events (kiota-dotnet) is the one ConnectWise's own apps use, which points to vendor automation, but we have not confirmed that with ConnectWise.

October 15, 03:44 to 03:49 UTC, one customer tenant: The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams (application ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) added itself to the Global Administrator role, then ran a Python script (User-Agent Python-urllib/3.12) that modified two other applications in the tenant: an MSP management application, and Huntress's own application (Huntress Security Platform), adding new client secrets to both. A followup attempt to add a certificate failed. The new secrets were set to expire in 2028.

October 15, 06:13 to 08:34 UTC: The app authenticated from 144.172.64[.]128 in 17 of the first 290~ tenants Huntress checked, across 17 different partner accounts.

Between October 13 and 14: The same address also made a scripted sign-in attempted using client application IDs belonging to other tools.

In the tenant where we saw persistence, the entire sequence took about five minutes. The ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams added itself to Global Administrator at 03:44 UTC and again at 03:48. In the same window it made nine changes to two other applications, an MSP management application and Huntress's own application. Six of the changes succeeded and three failed. One failure was a certificate credential that Microsoft rejected with a thumbprint mismatch, and the client secrets that were added afterward succeeded.

A client secret and a certificate are two ways for an application to prove its identity to Entra, and either one gives the holder the same access: sign in as that application, from anywhere, using the permissions already granted to it. App-only sign-ins involve no user, no device, and no MFA prompt. The person who creates a secret sees its value at creation, so the attacker holds working credentials for both applications until someone removes them. Adding credentials to an existing application is a known persistence technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1098.001, Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials).

The two applications that received new secrets are trusted, privileged tools. Adding a credential to an MSP management application can extend access beyond the one tenant, because those applications are often consented into the MSP's customers' tenants. A credential on a security tool's application gives the holder whatever that tool is permitted to do.

The Global Administrator change and the credential additions happened about two and a half hours before the first app authentications from 144.172.64[.]128 at 06:13 UTC. We have no source address for the earlier activity, so we have not tied the two phases to the same operator. User-Agents helped us distinguish vendor activity from attacker activity. The ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center applications we reviewed make their Graph calls with a .NET SDK User-Agent (kiota-dotnet). The application changes in the one tenant came from a Python User-Agent, and the password spray used curl/7.88.1. None of these is unique to this actor, and Python and curl are common in ordinary administration, so the combination of actor, operation, and User-Agent is the useful signal, not any single one.

Microsoft's audit log records role assignments and application changes along with the acting application, but for app-only actions it carries no source IP, and it does not record the details of the credential that was added or what an application read through Microsoft Graph. Confirming exactly what was added in a tenant takes the Entra audit log or a Graph query for that tenant, which is why we ask partners to review credentials directly.

What we have not confirmed

Impact. In the one tenant audit log we reviewed in detail, the actor shows no mail or file access. That does not mean no data was taken. Directory reads through Microsoft Graph leave no audit trail, so "tokens issued, nothing visible taken" is the current state.

Secondary app exposure. ConnectWise has multiple applications with very high-level permissions. In one customer tenant, Huntress confirmed that a second ConnectWise application, ConnectWise Cloud Management for Microsoft Teams, was used to grant itself Global Administrator and add credentials to other applications. We cannot verify that the remaining ConnectWise applications are secure.

What to do next

Disable the application now, even if you see nothing unusual.

In the Microsoft Entra admin center, go to Enterprise applications and search for Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (you can also search for "SkyKick" or "ConnectWise Cloud Backup").

Open Properties and set "Enabled for users to sign-in" to No.

Do not delete the application. Deleting it removes the consent, and you will need to re-consent to restore service.

Check for other ConnectWise and SkyKick applications in your tenant (search for "SkyKick" and "ConnectWise"). If you cannot verify one is safe, disable it as well, without deleting, until ConnectWise confirms that it is.

Application IDs to look for:

ConnectWise Cloud Backup 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae

ConnectWise Cloud Management2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83

ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640

ConnectWise Cloud Management - Exchange Online b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519

ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Graph 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827

ConnectWise Cloud Management - Partner Center412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e

ConnectWise Cloud Management - SharePoint Onlineb2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb

In older tenants the Cloud Management apps may appear as "SkyKick Cloud Manager."

If a ConnectWise or SkyKick application holds a directory role in your tenant, especially Global Administrator or Privileged Authentication Administrator, review it, and after the app is disabled remove any role you did not intentionally grant.

If you use Huntress, include the Huntress Security Platform application in the credential review above.

Review the credentials (client secrets and certificates) on all of your Enterprise applications and App registrations, especially management and security tools, for any added since October 13 that you did not create. Remove anything unexpected.

Check your Entra audit logs for ConnectWise or SkyKick applications adding themselves to a directory role, and if that application modifies other applications.

In those audit events, check the user agent. The ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center apps we reviewed make their Graph calls with a .NET SDK user agent (kiota-dotnet). The application changes we saw in the one tenant came from a Python user agent (Python-urllib/3.12), which differs from the vendor apps we reviewed.

Do not re-enable any ConnectWise applications until ConnectWise confirms all credentials have been reset.

Figure 2: Mitigation recommendations

Disabling the app pauses automated backups until it is re-enabled. Your emails, files, Teams messages, and user sign-ins keep working, and existing backups held by ConnectWise are not deleted. Consider whether a gap in recovery points matters for you.

If you want to check your logs:

In the Entra admin center, go to Monitoring > Sign-in logs, open the Service principal sign-ins tab, and filter by Application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae. The default User sign-ins tab will not show this data.

In the IP address column, look for any address outside Microsoft/Azure ranges. The app's normal egress is Azure private IPv6. Search for 144.172.64[.]128 specifically.

A clean result does not rule out access. Please disable the application regardless.

Also review Conditional Access: If any policy excludes this application, for example from a location-based block, the attacker's infrastructure will not be blocked there. Review those exclusions once the app is disabled.

Why this matters

The backup service needs broad access to do its job, and an attacker using its credentials will inherit that level of access for every tenant where the app is installed. Depending on the permissions in the tenant, that can include mailboxes, OneDrive and SharePoint files, Teams data, and directory information, much of it belonging to your clients. Some of that access, such as directory reads through Microsoft Graph, leaves no audit trail, which is why we suggest acting now instead of waiting for proof of access. The full potential impact depends on the permissions in play in each tenant.

What could happen

What an attacker can do with a credential like this depends on the permissions already granted to the application in each tenant. A backup service normally holds read access to mail, files, Teams, and directory data so it can copy them, and write access so it can restore them. An attacker holding tokens for that application inherits the same access: reading mail and files in bulk, downloading mailbox and OneDrive contents, enumerating users, groups, and applications, and, where write permissions exist, changing or deleting data. Because the access is app-only, it does not depend on a user being signed in, and the sign-in protections that apply to people do not apply to it.

The larger risk is what happens when that access is used to gain more. If an application can assign directory roles, as we saw in one tenant, it can make itself a Global Administrator, and an administrator can add credentials to other applications, create new applications and grant them permissions, reset passwords and authentication methods for users, and change Conditional Access policies. Each of those steps gives the attacker another way back in that does not depend on the original vendor credential, which is why rotating the vendor credential is necessary, but not enough.

In managed service provider environments the effect can compound. MSPs use management applications and delegated access to administer many customer tenants, so a foothold in one MSP tenant can become a path to its customers. We have not seen that happen, and the audit log shows changes, not reads, but it is the reason we ask MSPs to review credentials on their management and security tools first.

In ATT&CK terms, the activity we observed maps to valid cloud accounts (T1078.004) for the use of the vendor credential, additional cloud roles (T1098.003) for the self-assigned administrator roles, and additional cloud credentials (T1098.001) for the secrets added to other applications.

Detecting this in your own logs

These events appear in the Entra audit log as Add member to role, Update application, and Add service principal credentials. The fields that matter are the initiating application, the target, the result, and the user agent. A service principal that adds itself to a directory role, or that modifies other applications, is unusual in most tenants and worth investigating on its own.

Reducing exposure

Several Entra controls limit the damage if an application credential is stolen. Application management policies can restrict or block client secrets on app registrations and cap credential lifetimes. Limiting who holds the Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator roles reduces who can add credentials to applications. Conditional Access for workload identities, which needs additional licensing, can restrict where an application is allowed to sign in from, and Microsoft Entra ID Protection can flag risky service principals. None of these replaces reviewing credentials, but they make a planted secret harder to use or easier to spot.

What is Huntress Doing?

Huntress has been working with partners to address the steps above. We have also been:

Checking tenants where we can see sign-in logs through Microsoft Graph, and recording every public IP the app has signed in from.

That work is ongoing and will tell us who else is affected and whether other attacker IPs are involved.

We cannot check tenants without the necessary Entra licensing.

Disabling the application in tenants where we find activity from 144.172.64[.]128, and in tenants where a ConnectWise or SkyKick application gave itself a directory role, then notifying the affected partner.

Sweeping every tenant we can see for current state: ConnectWise and SkyKick service principals that hold privileged roles, and credentials added to any application since October 13, including our own application.

Looking at how we can add visibility into application sign-ins.

We will continue to update this blog as we learn more.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

Item

Description

144.172.64[.]128

Infrastructure used in the unauthorized activity Huntress observed a hosting provider (AS14956, RouterHosting). Used for the October 13 to 14 password spray and the October 15 app authentications.

144.172.64[.]99

Additional IP indicator shared by ConnectWise in its advisory (part of its update on 10/18 at 18:45 UTC).

144.172.64[.]60

Additional IP indicator shared by ConnectWise in its advisory (part of its update on 10/18 at 18:45 UTC).

506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae

Application ID of ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick Backup). This is a legitimate application. The credential for it is what was abused. Do not block the ID itself, disable the service principal in your tenant.

3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7

Application owner tenant ID seen on the app's service principal events (the vendor's tenant).

24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640

Application ID of ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams (formerly SkyKick Cloud Manager - MS Teams). This is a legitimate application. In one tenant it assigned itself Global Administrator and modified other applications. Do not block the ID itself, disable the service principal in your tenant.

Python-urllib/3.12

python-requests/2.31

User agents ConnectWise lists as observed on the suspicious authentication activity. Low fidelity on their own. Python-urllib/3.12 was also the user agent on the credential changes described above, but it is common and not unique to this activity.

curl/7.88.1

User agent seen on the password spray. Low fidelity on its own, but useful with the IP.

articles.title: Inside the Hunt: Sarah Reddish
articles.context: She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats
articles.full_text:
Meet Sarah Reddish, a Security Operations Analyst on Huntress' global Security Operations Center (SOC), working in Triage & Analysis. Her role goes far beyond monitoring a queue. She investigates and researches suspicious activity, intrusions, and a wide range of security threats. She also analyzes partner environments to determine what happened and what matters, and then writes clear reports with practical, easy-to-follow remediation guidance.

"I don't just identify threats," she says. "I translate them into clear reports and outcomes that help partners understand the risk and respond confidently." That means turning complex technical findings into information people can understand and act on, while helping protect partner data, systems, and peace of mind.

Sarah hanging with her Huntress teammates

A wider view of security operations

At Huntress, Sarah gets to work as part of a truly global SOC and protect a broad range of partner environments at scale. She collaborates across regions, participates in cross-region handoffs that support global SOC continuity, and learns from an exceptionally talented analyst community.

That global perspective changes what an investigation can become. Sarah isn't only working through a single environment or incident. From ambiguity to action

The most rewarding part of Sarah's work right now is turning complex, ambiguous threats into clear answers and actionable guidance. She investigates what happened, helps disrupt malicious activity, and sees her work directly wreck adversaries and improve our partners' security.

In one investigation, a fake browser-verification prompt instructed a user to run a command. Sarah traced the activity from the initial lure through execution and follow-on behavior, separating what she observed from what she could confirm. You investigate what happened, build attack timelines and scope, translate your findings and why they matter, and give partners clear remediation steps to protect themselves." Trust that stretches the role

His practical guidance, along with the trust he places in Sarah to own her work, has challenged her to think more strategically about both individual investigations and their broader impact.

That balance of support and ownership is an important part of how Sarah approaches the role. She is encouraged to work through difficult decisions, learn from an experienced global team, and consider not just what happened in an environment, but how her analysis can help a partner respond with confidence.

Stay curious and keep learning

For anyone considering a role like hers, Sarah's advice is direct: "Come ready to stay curious, think critically, and keep learning." The work is challenging and meaningful, with the opportunity to investigate real threats, communicate clearly, and learn alongside a talented global team.

articles.title: Huntress + AlgaPSA Integration: Built in Days by Nine Minds
articles.context: Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server
articles.full_text:
Over the past year, the Huntress API has grown from six read-only endpoints into a full integration and automation platform, along with Webhooks and an MCP server. For partners, that means Huntress data can show up wherever they already work, not just in our portal. It also means software vendors can build their own Huntress integrations on their own schedule, without having to wait on us.

Nine Minds is a great example. Their team built a Huntress integration for AlgaPSA, their professional services automation (PSA) platform, using our public API documentation. No technical support or special access needed. They just read the docs and, a few days later, had a working integration. This post covers what they built, what the experience was like, and what it shows about how you can use the Huntress API.

Meet Nine Minds and AlgaPSA

Nine Minds was founded by Robert Isaacs and Arnie Bellini, who both spent over a decade at ConnectWise. AlgaPSA is their answer to a problem they saw in the industry for years: PSA tools that are too expensive, too complicated, and primarily built for mature organizations.

AlgaPSA brings ticketing, projects, time tracking, billing, and client operations into one platform, and it was designed with the smallest MSPs in mind. As Robert told ChannelE2E, "The small MSP doesn't want to sign a three-year contract." But as they've progressed, larger MSPs have started taking notice, too.

AlgaPSA gives MSPs control over how they run the software with hosted, self-hosted, and open-source options. Over a hundred MSPs now rely on AlgaPSA for day-to-day operations, with more signing up every week.

Why Build a Huntress Integration?

For Nine Minds, the decision came down to two things. Mutual customers were asking for it, and their team spends a lot of time in the MSP community, including at IT Nation, and Huntress is one of the names they see everywhere.

When your users already rely on Huntress to catch threats, the next question is simple: how do those incidents get to the technicians who need to act on them? The AlgaPSA <> Huntress integration provides an answer.

How the Integration Works

The integration is built around the premise that a security incident should never go without a ticket. When the Huntress SOC publishes an incident report, it appears in AlgaPSA as a ticket on a dedicated security board, with the incident summary and a priority based on its severity.

Technicians work it like any other ticket, and the time they log flows into AlgaPSA's billing and invoicing. That means security responses get tracked and billed like the rest of their work, instead of living in a separate console. When the SOC closes the incident, the ticket can close automatically, too. And if an incident comes from a client that hasn't been mapped yet, it still lands on a triage board, so nothing slips through.

Setup takes a few steps:

Connect your Huntress API credentials

Map Huntress organizations to AlgaPSA clients

Choose where tickets land and how severities translate to priorities.

Nine Minds walks through each step in the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs.

A few things to know before you start:

Use a dedicated API key. Huntress API keys are tied to a user and mirror that user's permissions, so it's a good idea to create a separate key just for this integration.

You need AlgaPSA's paid tier. The Huntress integration is part of AlgaPSA's Enterprise Edition (also offered as AlgaPSA Pro). It isn't included in the open-source Community Edition.

Finish routing first. AlgaPSA won't start pulling incidents until the security board, the fallback client and board, and priorities for all three Huntress severities (Critical, High, and Low) are set.

Expect tickets on a schedule, not instantly. AlgaPSA checks Huntress for new incident reports at an interval you choose between one and 60 minutes, so tickets show up at the next check.

What Was It Like to Build on the Huntress API?

This is the part we're most excited about. Nine Minds went from idea to a shipped integration in just a few days.

They built it using our public documentation, without reaching out to us first. After a short period working out which data they needed, Robert said things went smoothly: no confusing fields, no missing endpoints, no documentation gaps that slowed them down. Their team also uses AI coding tools, and pointing those tools at the Huntress API docs was enough to get the job done.

"Integrating Huntress into AlgaPSA was easy enough that we almost felt as if we had missed something... [Then] our customers started thanking us for the integration. Working with Huntress could not have been easier."

– Robert IsaacsFounder / CEO, Nine Minds

Nine Minds also built a Huntress emulator so they could test the integration without depending on live incidents. They told us a dedicated sandbox environment would make that easier, and we've shared that feedback with our team.

What Else Can You Build?

AlgaPSA's integration shows one common pattern: pull incidents from Huntress and turn them into tickets. But the API supports a lot more.

A few examples:

Get incidents in real time. Instead of polling, Huntress Webhooks push incidents and escalations to your PSA, Slack, or SIEM as they happen.

Act on incidents. Approve or reject remediations through the Incident Report response API, and isolate or release hosts through the Agents API.

Automate onboarding. Create, update, and delete organizations programmatically. For example, when a new client is added in your RMM, automation can create the matching Huntress organization and start EDR deployment.

Reconcile billing and build reports. Pull billing reports and per-product organization stats, like agent counts, SIEM storage, and ITDR identity counts, into your dashboards, QBRs, or PSA contracts.

Bring Huntress into AI workflows. The Huntress MCP server connects your AI assistant to your incidents, agents, billing data, and more.

Prefer to see how this works? Watch our video below to see inside the Huntress API, Webooks, and MCP server:

Ready to Learn More?

AlgaPSA's integration started with a customer request and ended with a shipped feature just a few days later. That's the kind of experience we want every developer to have with the Huntress API. If you've been thinking about connecting Huntress to your own tools, the docs are a good place to start.

Build on the Huntress API: Start with the Huntress API docs.

Use Huntress with AlgaPSA: See the AlgaPSA Huntress integration docs for setup steps.

Share feedback: Have an idea for an endpoint, webhook, or integration? Add it to our Integrations, Webhooks, and APIs feedback board.

articles.title: What Does the Dark Web Look Like? Pulling Back the Curtain | Huntress
articles.context: Avoid downloads and scripts: Avoid downloading unknown files, especially on the dark web, and disable scripts like JavaScript in Tor's settings—they can be exploited to reveal...
articles.full_text:
In today’s always-connected world, the line between dark and light is blurring.

Well, actually, you’re still protected from finding out what the dark web looks like because you need to download a special browser to access it. But the drama of the dark web can be intriguing. And it’s not all wicked criminal activity either.

Curious about what’s lurking in the shadows of the internet? Keep reading to learn more about the state of the dark web, what it is, and how to access it (safely, of course!).

What is the dark web?

Everyone has their own preconceived notion of what the dark web is. (Of course, with a name as ominous as dark web, it kind of sets the mood, right?) For the sake of this blog, we focused on finding a credible definition that isn’t muddied with preconceptions.

The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that you can only reach with special tools. Merriam-Webster describes it as a set of sites that search engines don't index and that regular browsers can't open. Reaching them takes specialized software or a specific network setup, and encryption keeps both site owners and visitors anonymous.

(If you were expecting a more sinister-sounding definition for the term dark web, you’re not alone. 😅)

The web, as a whole, can be divided into three parts: the surface web vs. deep web vs. dark web:

Dark web: This is where things get…different. As we said, dark web activity isn't indexed and requires special software or network configuration to access. While it can be a place where people broker illegal activities, it can also be used for legal activities, like anonymously sourcing information.

Surface web: The surface web is everything that’s automatically indexed by search engines. It’s everything that pops up when you Google something (or Bing or whatever search engine), and you don’t need any sort of special software or login to access it.

Deep web: The deep web is sites that are not indexed, but are accessible to the average person, usually through encryption or password protection (or both, both is good!). This includes things like online banking and cloud storage.
