articles.title: Texas HB 3834 Cybersecurity & AI Training Requirements
articles.context: In August 2019, the computer systems of 23 Texas municipalities were hit with a ransomware cyber attack that locked access to all computer files in one instance
articles.full_text:
Did you know that Texas passed a new regulation for state employees to participate in a mandatory cyber security awareness training program?

In June of 2019, Texas State Legislature passed HB 3834, a bill requiring local and state government employees, and even state contractors, to complete a Department of Information Resources (DIR) approved cyber security awareness training program like Huntress! Hint: We’ve made security awareness training more flavorful than your favorite steak house!

Depending on your organization’s role as a state agency, local government entity, or contractor, you may be immediately impacted by this annual compliance training requirement, known as HB 3834. If your organization falls into scope, HB 3834 requires that a security awareness training program has been rolled out and completed by all required employees every year, with your organization certifying completion to DIR by August 31st. That’s a pretty big burden if you haven’t established a formal security awareness training program yet.

And there’s a new factor. As of September 1, 2025, HB 3512 added a second annual requirement for the same people: a DIR-certified artificial intelligence (AI) awareness training. In-scope employees now need to complete both cybersecurity and AI awareness training each year.

But don’t worry, we are going to show you what is required, why this regulation came to be, and how you can comply with HB 3834 without stressing out.

Why is the HB 3834 Regulation Necessary?

It’s no secret that governments are now prime targets for hackers more than ever. In August 2019, the computer systems of 23 Texas municipalities were hit with a ransomware cyber attack that locked access to all computer files in one instance. The ransomware even revoked the ability to process utility payments in another municipality. The Mayor of one unnamed Texas city came forward with claims the hacker demanded $2.5 million in ransom. It goes without saying that the Lone Star State is no exception and hackers are officially messing with Texas.

Now is the time to make a change. With the human element involved in 62% of breaches, according to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, it’s no secret that a strong security awareness program is the key to staying out of the news headlines.

It’s time to fight back, Texas. It’s time to train your employees on how to defend themselves and beat the hackers.

How do I Comply With the HB 3834 Cyber Security Awareness Training Requirements?

HB 3834 is in full force and all state agencies, local governments, and contractors need to complete their compliance training each year. Let’s look at the steps you need to take to get you and your team compliant with the HB 3834 cyber security training requirements. And if you are looking for advice on building your security awareness training program for HB 3834, our expert security awareness team is happy to help.

Texas HB 3834 Scope

Step 1: Are you in Scope?

First step is to determine if your organization is in scope of HB 3834. If you are reading this, you probably already have a hunch that you may be. To confirm, the personnel in scope of HB 3834 cyber security awareness training compliance applies to state agency, local government, and even contractor employees throughout the state of Texas.

State Agencies – Employees who use a computer to complete at least 25 percent of the employee’s required duties, and elected or appointed officers of the agency.

Local Government Entities – Employees and elected or appointed officials who have access to a local government computer system or database and use a computer to perform at least 25 percent of their duties. For school districts, only the district’s cybersecurity coordinator is required to complete the annual training. Other school district employees complete it as determined by the district, with the coordinator.

Contractors of State Agencies – Those contractors who have access to a state computer system or database must complete training during the term of the contract and during any renewal period. There are no exceptions for state agency contractors.

Employees and officials on certain types of extended leave (military or FMLA leave, for example) are exempt as long as they no longer have access to the organization’s systems and databases.

Step 2: Choose a State Certified Vendor

Now that you have confirmed your scope, you must choose a security awareness training vendor that is certified by the State of Texas, such as Huntress. Certified vendors must complete a rigorous training content assessment, certify with the State of Texas that their training program meets all cyber education requirements, and ensure that those requirements are upheld on a continuous basis year over year. Certifications expire every August 31 and have to be renewed annually, so make sure your vendor is certified for the current fiscal year. Simply put, selecting a vendor that’s already done the heavy lifting is required to get started.

With Huntress Managed SAT, you can satisfy the cybersecurity requirement using our Intro to Cybersecurity, Infosecurity, and Texas-specific episodes in our library. Most people can finish them in less than 30 minutes.

The AI requirement works a little differently. Thanks to the free, certified AI awareness training video on YouTube provided by DIR, you can also satisfy the AI requirements via Huntress Managed SAT as well. All you need to do is create a custom episode in Huntress Managed SAT, add the video, and include one question: “Did you complete it?” That way, completion gets tracked right alongside the rest of your training.

Step 3: Launch your Program

Okay so you picked your vendor, but now you need to launch the cyber security training program to your employees. It’s critical to communicate how important completing this required training is. If your employees don’t understand why they are required to participate in this training, they won’t have the motivation you need to have it completed. Motivation is a key component of getting your cyber security training program off the ground and supported by employees.

Step 4: Ensure Completion

Now that you have launched your training program, that doesn’t mean you are done. As part of HB 3834, you need to ensure your employees complete the required cyber security training. Remember it’s important to discuss how this cyber security training program will help your employees become more cyber-savvy both at work and at home. Make it fun by promoting the training across your organization similar to a marketing campaign. This will help drive completion records, and you may even offer incentives for early completion.

Once everyone is done, state agencies and local governments must certify their compliance to DIR by August 31 using DIR’s online certification form. You don’t send DIR individual training records or certificates, but you do need to keep your own, so hang on to those completion reports.

Step 5: Keep it Going

Congrats, you’ve finished your first round of security awareness training! This is a big accomplishment, but the party doesn’t stop here. Remember that you need to keep this momentum going. The best way to do that is to reinforce your security culture to help make security top of mind. Once a year security awareness training is not going to stop the hackers. You need to continue this effort throughout the year, using different methods to communicate and reinforce security concepts in every employee’s mind.

What NOT to do with HB 3834

Although it’s easy to recognize HB 3834 as another compliance regulation to just check the box, it shouldn’t be.

The consequences of falling victim to a cyber attack are well known and your focus should be to ensure all employees understand the risks they face.

You don’t want to be tomorrow’s news headline and your employees are your first step as the most powerful defense for your organization. A strong cyber security training program is the key to protect beyond the regulations of HB 3834. Remember we are all working towards a common goal to beat the hackers, not the regulations.

Ready to check the HB 3834 box without the snooze fest? See how Huntress Managed SAT helps you meet Texas HB 3834 requirements in less than 30 minutes.

articles.title: Fake WatchGuard VPN Site Steals Credentials
articles.context: ]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware
articles.full_text: Acknowledgments: Thanks to Stephanie Fairless and Andrew Brandt for their help in analysing this attack. Background A simple search on Google or Bing for a VPN client download may seem like a run-of-the-mill task, but it can also expose users to convincing credential phishing sites. In January 2026, WatchGuard's Secplicity team published research into a credential-harvesting campaign targeting VPN providers, covering lookalike download sites for WatchGuard, F5, Fortinet, SonicWall, and Sophos clients. This campaign included two domains impersonating WatchGuard itself: watchguard-vpn[.]com and watchguard-vpn[.]net. The findings included a .NET executable posing as their Mobile VPN with SSL application, served from a GitHub repository, that sent entered credentials to a command-and-control (C2) server. Researchers said they also observed Bing's Copilot recommending watchguard-vpn[.]net when asked about "watchguard vpn," although at the time of their research that domain had "no backend logic to direct users to the spoofed downloads page." Two months later, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported activity linked specifically to watchguard-vpn[.]com. Microsoft attributed this wider campaign iteration to Storm-2561, a financially motivated actor that has been active since May 2025. The attack chain highlighted by Microsoft involved pushing spoofed vendor sites up the search results, delivering a signed, fake MSI that sideloads malicious DLLs, harvesting credentials typed into a fake client, and then showing an installation error and pointing the victim to the real vendor download so nothing looks wrong afterwards. Fast forward to October: the Huntress SOC analyzed an incident that involved one of the initial domains that WatchGuard had reported back in January – watchguard-vpn[.]net – that was consistent with previous reports of this credential-theft campaign targeting WatchGuard VPN credentials. However, further investigation into the incident showed that this latest iteration of the attack chain is slightly different. Rather than downloading a fake client, the domain instead downloads a genuine, validly signed WatchGuard installer. As of October 13, the main domain linked to the activity Huntress observed (watchguard-vpn[.]net) was offline. Prior to publishing, Huntress notified WatchGuard about this active campaign and shared the relevant infrastructure details. Figure 1: End-to-end flow of the WatchGuard VPN credential phish. Technical Details Initial access: A typo and a search engine On October 7, Huntress Managed Defender flagged suspicious activity that stemmed back to activity from a user account at a managed service provider. Further investigation into the incident revealed that an administrator had searched Bing for "watchguard vpn sll download." Eight seconds later, they clicked through to www.watchguard-vpn[.]net, a page titled "WatchGuard Firebox VPN Client." The click went through Bing's standard bing.com/ck/a result redirect, with the destination encoded in the u= parameter (aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud2F0Y2hndWFyZC12cG4ubmV0Lw decodes to hxxps://www.watchguard-vpn[.]net/). This redirect is consistent with a standard Bing search-result click and, alongside the lookalike domain's apparent search-result placement, supports classifying the lure as SEO poisoning rather than malvertising. Secplicity and Microsoft have also described related activity in this campaign as SEO poisoning. Figure 2: The lookalike domain for a routine VPN download search. We took a closer look at watchguard-vpn[.]net as part of our investigation. The malicious domain Video: The attack chain When targets arrive at watchguard-vpn[.]net, they see a domain that pretends to be the legitimate WatchGuard website, and offers an option to "Download WatchGuard SSL VPN." The fake WatchGuard website also includes information about WatchGuard products and a "WatchGuard Mobile VPN Questions" section (likely meant to bolster SEO ranking). Ironically, at the bottom of the page, the website includes the disclaimer: "An independent English-language fan site about WatchGuard Mobile VPN. Not an official sales, download, or support channel." Figures 3 and 4: The malicious domain (left) versus the actual legitimate WatchGuard domain (right) When targets click through the site, they are sent to the download page at watchguard-vpn[.]net/index.php, which poses as a "WatchGuard Support Page" and gives several options for downloading the VPN for different OS configurations. Credential capture: Inside popup.js Clicking on any of the download options presents victims with a pop-up prompt that reads "To install WatchGuard SSL VPN, please enter your connection details" and asks for three things: Server, Login, and Password. The phishing logic lives in a single file, popup.js, about 150 lines of plain, unobfuscated JavaScript. Figures 5 and 6: Targets are taken to a download page (left) and when they click "Download" the credential prompt is shown (right) The legitimate Mobile VPN with SSL client also asks for these three values when users connect, so the prompt looks reasonable. Notably, the "Server" field is particularly useful for the attacker—it gives them the VPN server's address that they can authenticate to. The submission handler sends the form contents to the collection domain: Loading Gist... The user's typed input is wrapped in JSON and posted to watchguard-ssl[.]online, tagged to indicate whether this is the first or second attempt. The fetch is wrapped in a try/catch statement that only logs a console warning on failure, so even if the collector is down, the user sees nothing unusual. Interestingly, the attack chain purposefully rejects the first submission into this pop-up from the target. The script clears all three fields and replaces the header with red text: headerText.innerHTML = 'Incorrect data, please enter again to start installation'; attempt = 2; Anyone who mistyped their passwords will now type more carefully, and anyone unsure which of their passwords applies is likely to try the other one, so the attacker gets a second set of credentials to validate against, with the attempt tag marking which submission came last. Figures 7 and 8: The forced "Incorrect data" message after the first submission (left) and then the second prompt (right) The twist: The payload is the real thing After the second submission, the pop-up turns green ("VPN client installation has started"), and the script creates a hidden link and clicks it: const DOWNLOAD_FILE = 'https://cdn.watchguard.com/SoftwareCenter/Files/MUVPN_SSL/12_11_5/WG-MVPN-SSL_12_11_5.exe'; This is WatchGuard's official CDN. The file is a Inno Setup installer for "Mobile VPN with SSL client", version 12.11.5, copyright WatchGuard Technologies. It carries an Authenticode signature from WatchGuard Technologies, Inc., issued by Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36, with a countersignature timestamp of 4 November 2025. We recomputed the Authenticode SHA256 digest of the file (fb3c39ba…0032ac1f) and it matches the digest in the signature, so the binary has not been modified since WatchGuard signed it. For attackers, the use of a real, signed VPN client makes the phishing attack far more convincing, and more difficult to detect. First of all, there's no trojanized installer or malicious DLL for security defenses to flag. Second of all, victims are still getting their expected outcome. Because they're still getting an actual installer, this alleviates any suspicions. This is a twist on the same idea in the attack chain that Microsoft highlighted, where attackers sent the victim to the real installer afterwards so nothing looks wrong—but now with the fake client removed from the middle. In the particular case that we investigated, the browser history actually recorded no download from cdn.watchguard.com for the timeframe in question. Because the script only triggers the download after the second submission, this suggests the user did not complete both rounds, although they may have entered their credentials in the first round. Huntress Managed Defender flagged the incident 21 seconds after the malicious domain loaded, and the SOC was able to provide the organization with remediation steps before the attack could escalate. Old domain, new backend The WHOIS record for watchguard-vpn[.]net shows a creation date of August 22, 2026, with Realtime Register B.V. as registrar. Secplicity recorded the same domain in January resolving to 74.208.236[.]39; as of October 9 it resolves to 80.249.132[.]140 on Site BV hosting (LeaseWeb Netherlands, AS60781). This indicates the domain was registered again after WatchGuard's January observation, but available evidence does not establish whether the same operators controlled both registrations. The current iteration hosted a working credential-harvesting flow. The credential collection endpoint, watchguard-ssl[.]online, was registered through Dynadot on September 14, 2026 and resolves to 158.94.209[.]19 (Omegatech LTD, AS202412, Amsterdam). The table below outlines an infrastructure timeline for the lure and collection domains. Date (UTC) Event Jan 13 2026 Secplicity reports watchguard-vpn[.]net (then 74.208.236[.]39) with no backend Aug 22 2026 watchguard-vpn[.]net (resolving to resolves to 80.249.132[.]140) registered (Realtime Register B.V.) Sep 14 2026 watchguard-ssl[.]online registered (Dynadot) Sep 17 and 22 2026 urlscan.io submissions of watchguard-vpn[.]net Oct 7 2026 Victim lands on www.watchguard-vpn[.]net As of October 8, detections for the domains linked to this attack were thin, which is not totally surprising given that the domains weren't actually deploying malware. Only seven VirusTotal vendors flagged the lure domain, and two flagged the collector, with no AbuseIPDB reports against either IP. Conclusion This attack chain raises the bar by removing the malware component and making it harder to detect. The operators give victims a convincing installation experience while bypassing many endpoint-focused security controls, through collecting VPN credentials in the browser and then delivering the legitimate, signed WatchGuard installer from WatchGuard's own CDN. If you think you entered credentials on this or a similar site, you should immediately reset the password for every affected account and treat the VPN endpoint associated with those credentials as known to the attacker. Defenders should also enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on top of a username and password. Monitor for SSL VPN logins from hosting providers, unfamiliar ASNs, or countries where the account has never connected from. Defenders should also block watchguard-vpn[.]net and watchguard-ssl[.]online as well as the IPs outlined in the IOC section below. Finally, defenders should publish (and bookmark) official VPN-client download links, including software.watchguard.com, in client documentation. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) Item Description watchguard-vpn[.]net Lookalike WatchGuard VPN download page hosting the credential modal (registered 2026-08-22) 80.249.132[.]140 Lure hosting, Site BV / LeaseWeb Netherlands (AS60781) watchguard-ssl[.]online Credential collection endpoint receiving JSON POSTs (registered 2026-09-14) 158.94.209[.]19 Collector hosting, Omegatech LTD (AS202412), Amsterdam popup.js Credential capture modal script; fields server, login, password, attempt

articles.full_text:
Most cyber threats start out small and unassuming before they turn into the OH $#!T moments that put your whole business at risk. They can creep up fast during a normal day with a website you trust and a habit you don't question. You ask your favorite AI platform for help, follow "fix it" instructions when it hits a snag, and get back to work without thinking twice.

Nothing feels risky on the surface. But underneath, the "normal" AI search result you clicked and the "fix it" instructions you followed just helped an attacker gain access to your Microsoft 365 account. While you move on to the next task in your day, they walk straight into your inbox without a password or MFA prompt, looking just like you. They read through your messages and create hidden inbox rules that hide their tracks. That stealthy intrusion is mailbox manipulation, and in this case, it can escalate into full-blown business email compromise (BEC) within hours.

Threats like AI platform abuse and ClickFix-style attacks on their own can feel like small problems. Chained together, they give an attacker everything they need to set up an OH $#!T moment that no one sees coming until it's too late.

Meet Doris and her ClickFix problem

Principal Product Researcher Truman Kain shows what this looks like in practice and how easily it blends into a normal workflow.

Meet Doris Stewart, a fictional finance employee at a company called Speedway Laundry, owned by Speedway Industries. Doris wants help responding to an email, so she goes to Google and searches for ChatGPT. She clicks what appears to be a normal sponsored result and, unknowingly, lands on a custom attacker-built GPT. But there are no obvious tells that this custom GPT is malicious. And Doris trusts ChatGPT, which is what the attacker was banking on.

Here's where things start to get sketchy. The custom GPT tells her there's a service issue and sends her to a fake verification page. Doris is prompted to press Command+Space, paste a command into Terminal, and press Enter. She doesn't recognize that this is a ClickFix scam, and by following those steps, the attacker has tricked her into compromising her own machine.

Now, the attacker runs a script to retrieve cookies and spots Doris' Microsoft session cookie, the one that keeps her logged in to Outlook without entering a password or MFA code each time she needs access. By dropping that cookie into a fresh browser using a free extension and refreshing the page, the attacker is now sitting in Doris' inbox with full control. There was no password and no MFA prompt to get past. The session was already authenticated, so the stolen cookie did the work.

This is where the attacker turns access into cash. In Doris' inbox, the attacker finds an invoice awaiting approval, creates an inbox rule named ".." so it gets easily overlooked, and sets it to archive any message containing the invoice number. Then the attacker replies to Treasury as Doris, asking them to send the payment to a new routing number, deletes the sent message to hide the evidence, and empties the trash. Doris never sees any of it, and the whole thing unfolds in about 24 hours.

This attack didn't require lots of time, money, or technical know-how. But it worked fast, and Doris will be left cleaning up a financial mess that she didn't even know existed.

How Doris could have avoided trouble

The good news is that knowing where to break links in the attack chain can stop a bigger business disruption from happening. In this case, on the endpoint side, the initial access shows up as a Mac shell running curl output with the attacker's IP address Base64-encoded inside it, the exact command Doris walked through pasting into Terminal a few minutes earlier. That pattern is worth flagging as suspicious on endpoints until proven otherwise.

On the identity side, the tells are just as suspicious. Two browsers are active in one session; there are two different operating systems tied to the same login; traffic is routed through a VPN with no business reason to be there; and that sketchy, almost invisible inbox rule ("..").

This isn't new tradecraft, but it's effective and convenient for attackers to slip in unnoticed without dropping noisy tooling that'll get flagged by managed security tools.

Getting ahead of OH $#!T moments with the Tragic Quadrant

The Huntress Tragic Quadrant plots threats on two axes, including the ones in this exact attack chain. The x-axis (prevalence) shows how often we see them in the environments we monitor, and the y-axis, or as we all call it, "pucker factor" (which, if you've ever been on the receiving end of these attacks, makes perfect sense), shows how much damage they cause when they land. That view helps you tackle the riskiest gaps first, so you don't end up in an OH $#!T moment like Doris.

On the lower quadrants, you see tactics like AI platform abuse and ClickFix that aren't usually catastrophic on their own, even if we see them often in our telemetry. The real risk happens when attackers chain them together, and the arrows move up and to the right into the OH $#!T quadrant, where a hidden inbox rule can turn into much bigger problems like BEC or ransomware.

When you know which corner a tactic falls into, it gets easier to see which threats deserve your focus right now and how to spot them in your environment.

articles.full_text:
Differences between legacy self-assessments (DFARS 252.204-7019) and CMMC Level 2 self-assessments (DFARS 252.204-7021) are leading defense contractors to a rude awakening: they no longer dictate the requirements they can implement or defer during a NIST 800-171 implementation. Identifying the “non-negotiable” requirements dictated by the CMMC program avoids future scenarios where a single missing requirement voids contract award eligibility or exposes the organization to the False Claims Act.

Old vs. New CMMC Level 2 Requirements

Self-assessments performed under the DFARS 252.204-7019 (Notice of NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Requirements) and DFARS 252.204-7020 allowed contractors to report any score, ranging from a "haven't even started" score of -203 to a perfect 110 points, using the DoD Assessment Methodology (DoDAM).

CMMC Level 2 self-assessments are scored using the DOD CMMC scoring methodology, and DFARS 252.204-7997 (which replaces both 252.204-7019 and 252.204-7020 under the DFARS overhaul) now points government DIBCAC assessments at that same methodology.

The real difficulty emerges when you pair CMMC point values with self-assessment requirements from the DFARS 252.204-7021 CMMC clause. Now your CMMC self-assessment has a minimum score that isn't evident in the contract clause language itself.

The New Bare Minimum

Completing a CMMC Level 2 self-assessment uses the same assessment objectives and point values as previous self-assessment procedures, but there are some tough mandates buried in 32 CFR 170.21, which sets the bar for a Conditional Level 2 (Self) status:

Your self-assessment score must be at least 80% of the 110 requirements in the model, or 88

You must implement all requirements worth three (3) or five (5) points

Additionally, a short list of one point requirements must also be implemented

These non-negotiable requirements from NIST 800-171 yield a self-assessment score of 64, and represent 85% of all possible points in the scoring methodology. This means your only real flexibility when achieving CMMC Level 2 is deciding which 24 (of the remaining 46) one-point requirements you'll implement to reach a minimum score of 88 on your first self-assessment submitted to the Department's Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS).

A Ticking Clock

With 32 CFR 170.21 putting a new floor on minimum compliance, it's important to understand how quickly the "ceiling" approaches because of how "POA&M closeout" works in the CMMC rules. Under CMMC self-assessment requirements, submitting a CMMC Level 2 self-assessment with any unmet requirements kickstarts a 180-day period to close out those remaining items. Failing to complete those items and update CMMC Status in SPRS will cause that Conditional status to expire after 180 days.

Any contractor submitting a less-than-perfect Level 2 self-assessment should be aware of this mechanism, since it causes self-assessments to expire earlier than normal. Don't end up in a situation where your affirming official logs into SPRS to submit their annual affirmation, only to find your self-assessment has expired, silently disqualifying the company for bids they may have submitted during that timeframe.

How Huntress Helps

Some NIST 800-171 requirements call for specialized capabilities—not just written policies—including ongoing system monitoring, security-event logging and review, threat detection, and incident handling. Huntress brings together endpoint and identity detection and response, security-event collection and retention, and 24/7 SOC monitoring to help organizations operationalize requirements across audit and accountability, incident response, security-control monitoring, and system integrity. We also map our products to applicable CMMC controls and provide assessor-ready documentation, but each organization must still configure these capabilities for its environment, integrate them into its response processes, and maintain evidence that each in-scope requirement is met.

Of the 55 requirements currently documented in Huntress CMMC resources: 32 are non-negotiable. Overall, the requirements addressed in the Huntress Shared Responsibility Matrix (SRM) add up to 164 points in the Level 2 scoring methodology, or 52 percent of all possible points.

As we launch new capabilities, expect Huntress to contribute towards more 800-171 requirements and yield more possible points.

Conclusion

When a solicitation or contract requires CMMC Level 2 (Self), a current Level 2 (Self) status and an affirmation in SPRS are a condition of contract award, and that status will require an implementation score of at least 88 with every non-POA&M-able requirement met. Contractors should respond to this heightened requirement quickly, completing NIST 800-171 implementations and submitting new CMMC Level 2 (Self) assessment in SPRS before the lack of an assessment entry costs them a contract award or contract option.
